chunks.text:
Testing Your API — Why this matters

A pilot runs through a checklist before every flight, even though the plane flew fine yesterday. Something might have changed overnight, and the checklist catches it before take-off rather than in the air.

Automated API tests are that checklist. You write them once, and they run on every change. They catch **regressions**: features that used to work and silently broke when someone edited nearby code. They also act as **living documentation**: a test called "Alice cannot delete Bob's task" states the rule precisely and proves it still holds.

"It worked when I tried it in the browser" is not proof. You tried one request, as one user, on one day, and probably only the case where everything goes right. A test suite tries dozens of cases, including the nasty ones, every time, in seconds.

chunks.text:
Testing Your API — What an API test asserts

An API test sends a real HTTP request and then **asserts** (checks) facts about what happened. There are four things worth checking:

1. **Status code**: `201`, `404`, `401`... The most basic check, and never enough on its own.
2. **Body**: the JSON contains the right fields and values, e.g. `title` is `"Buy milk"` and `done` is `false`; error responses have the expected Problem Details `type` and field errors.
3. **Headers**: e.g. `Content-Type: application/json`, a `Location` header after a `201`, or `Allow` on a `405`.
4. **Side effects**: what changed (or did not change) in the database. A `201` response is meaningless if no row was written, and a rejected request is a bug if it wrote a row anyway.

```text
assert status == 201
assert body.title == "Buy milk"
assert header "Content-Type" starts with "application/json"
assert database has 1 task with title "Buy milk" and owner_id 123
```

Reference (not copied): Ham Vocke, The Practical Test Pyramid (https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html).

chunks.text:
Testing Your API — Happy path vs failure cases

The **happy path** is the case where everything is correct: a valid user sends a valid request and it succeeds. Beginners test this and stop.

**Failure cases** (sometimes called sad paths or edge cases) are everything else: missing fields, wrong types, values at the limit, the wrong user, no token, an expired token, an id that does not exist. Most real bugs hide here, because developers write code thinking about the happy path, and failure cases are the ones they forgot. Attackers live entirely in the failure cases.

For one endpoint, `POST /tasks`, a fair split looks like this:

| Happy path | Failure cases |
|---|---|
| valid title, no due date | title missing, empty, 201 characters |
| valid title, future due date | due date in the past, `2026-02-30` |
| | `done` is `"yes"`; body is not JSON |
| | no token; expired token; extra `owner_id` field |

Expect several failure tests for each happy-path test.

chunks.text:
Testing Your API — Unit, integration and end-to-end tests

Tests differ in how much of the system they exercise.

- **Unit test**: checks one small piece of logic in isolation, without HTTP or a real database. Example: a function `validate_task(body)` returns an error for a 201-character title. Very fast; thousands run in seconds.
- **Integration test**: checks that your code works together with a real external part, such as the PostgreSQL database. Example: send `POST /tasks` to a running TaskFlow server backed by a test database, then query the `tasks` table. Slower, but proves the pieces fit.
- **End-to-end (E2E) test**: drives the whole deployed system the way a user does, for example a browser opening the TaskFlow web app, logging in as Alice and creating a task through the form. Slowest and most fragile, but closest to reality.

Most tests in this unit are integration tests at the API level: they send real HTTP requests and check the database.

chunks.text:
Testing Your API — The test pyramid

The **test pyramid** (popularised by Mike Cohn and explained in Martin Fowler's site article "The Practical Test Pyramid") is a guide to how many tests of each kind to write:

```text
        /\        few   end-to-end   (slow, fragile, realistic)
       /  \
      /----\      some  integration  (real HTTP + test database)
     /      \
    /--------\    many  unit         (fast, focused)
```

Why this shape? Unit tests are cheap to write, fast to run and point straight at the broken line. E2E tests are slow, break for unrelated reasons (a button moved) and are expensive to maintain, so keep only a few for the most important journeys, such as "sign in and create a task".

The opposite shape, mostly manual or E2E tests and few unit tests, is sometimes called the "ice-cream cone" and leads to slow, unreliable feedback. A useful rule: test each thing at the lowest level that can catch the bug.

chunks.text:
Testing Your API — Arrange, act, assert

Good tests share one simple structure, called **arrange–act–assert** (or given–when–then):

1. **Arrange**: set up the world the test needs. Create users, tasks and tokens.
2. **Act**: do exactly one thing, usually send one HTTP request.
3. **Assert**: check the status, body, headers and side effects.

```text
test "deleting a task removes it":
    # Arrange
    alice = create_user(id=123, email="alice@example.com")
    task  = create_task(owner=alice, title="Old note")
    token = login_token(alice)

    # Act
    res = DELETE "/v1/tasks/{task.id}" with Bearer token

    # Assert
    assert res.status == 204
    assert db.count("SELECT count(*) FROM tasks WHERE id = $1", task.id) == 0
```

Keeping the three parts visibly separate makes a failing test easy to read: you can see what was set up, what was done, and which expectation failed. One test should check one behaviour.

chunks.text:
Testing Your API — Worked example: creating a task

Goal: prove that `POST /tasks` creates a task owned by the caller.

**Arrange.** Insert Alice into an empty test database and get her a token:

```sql
INSERT INTO users (id, email, password_hash, name)
VALUES (123, 'alice@example.com', '<hash>', 'Alice');
```

**Act.** Send one request:

```http
POST /v1/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Authorization: Bearer <alice-token>
Content-Type: application/json

{"title": "Buy milk"}
```

**Assert** on what came back and what changed:

```http
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /v1/tasks/1
Content-Type: application/json

{"id": 1, "title": "Buy milk", "done": false, "due_date": null, "created_at": "2026-10-14T09:00:00Z"}
```

```text
assert status == 201
assert body.title == "Buy milk" and body.done == false
assert header Location == "/v1/tasks/" + body.id
row = SELECT owner_id, title FROM tasks WHERE id = body.id
assert row exists and row.owner_id == 123
```

The final check is the important one: the default `done = false` and `owner_id = 123` came from the server, not the client.

chunks.text:
Testing Your API — Worked example: testing validation boundaries

Validation bugs cluster at the **boundaries** of a rule. TaskFlow's rule is "title is 1–200 characters", so test just inside and just outside each edge:

| Test | Title sent | Expected |
|---|---|---|
| missing title | (field absent) | 422, error at `#/title` |
| empty | `""` | 422 |
| minimum | `"a"` (1 char) | 201 |
| maximum | 200 × `"a"` | 201 |
| one over | 201 × `"a"` | 422 |

A classic bug is writing `length < 200` instead of `length <= 200`; only the 200-character test catches it.

```text
test "title of 201 characters is rejected":
    # Arrange
    alice = create_user(123); token = login_token(alice)
    # Act
    res = POST "/v1/tasks" {"title": repeat("a", 201)} with token
    # Assert
    assert res.status == 422
    assert res.body.errors[0].pointer == "#/title"
    assert db.count("SELECT count(*) FROM tasks") == 0
```

The last line matters: a rejected request must not leave a half-created row behind.

Reference (not copied): Ham Vocke, The Practical Test Pyramid (https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html).

chunks.text:
Testing Your API — Testing 404s

A missing resource must give `404 Not Found`, not a `500` crash and not a `200` with `null`. Pick an id that certainly does not exist in the test database:

```text
test "getting a task that does not exist returns 404":
    alice = create_user(123); token = login_token(alice)
    res = GET "/v1/tasks/999999" with token
    assert res.status == 404
    assert res.header "Content-Type" starts with "application/problem+json"
    assert res.body.type == "https://api.taskflow.example/problems/not-found"
```

Repeat for every method that takes an id: `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` on `/tasks/999999` should also return 404, and none should create a row (a `PUT` to a missing id in TaskFlow does not create a task).

Also test the contrast case: `GET /tasks?done=true` for a user with no finished tasks must return `200` with `[]`, not 404. A malformed id such as `/tasks/abc` is another useful test: it should be a clean 4xx, never a 500 caused by a database type error.

Reference (not copied): Ham Vocke, The Practical Test Pyramid (https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html).

chunks.text:
Testing Your API — Worked example: testing authentication

Authentication tests check that the API refuses requests that don't prove who the caller is. **401 Unauthorized** means "not authenticated": no valid credentials.

**Case 1: no token.**

```http
GET /v1/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example

HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer
```

**Case 2: an expired token.** Arrange a token for Alice whose expiry time is in the past (most test setups can mint one directly, rather than waiting for real time to pass).

```text
test "expired token is rejected":
    alice = create_user(123)
    token = make_token(alice, expires_at = now - 1 minute)
    res = POST "/v1/tasks" {"title": "Sneaky"} with token
    assert res.status == 401
    assert db.count("SELECT count(*) FROM tasks") == 0
```

Add a third case for a token whose signature has been tampered with. Every protected endpoint needs these tests, not just one; a forgotten check on `DELETE` is exactly the kind of bug they exist to catch.

chunks.section: Worked example: Alice tries Bob's task
chunks.text:
Testing Your API — Worked example: Alice tries Bob's task

Authorization tests check that an authenticated user can only touch their own data. OWASP's testing guide for **insecure direct object references (IDOR)** recommends using at least two test users and swapping an object id from one user into the other user's request.

**Arrange.** Alice (123) and Bob (456) each exist. Bob owns task 77:

```sql
INSERT INTO tasks (id, owner_id, title, done)
VALUES (77, 456, 'Bob''s secret plan', false);
```

**Act.** With Alice's valid token, try every method on task 77:

```http
GET /v1/tasks/77 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Authorization: Bearer <alice-token>
```

then `PATCH /v1/tasks/77` with `{"done": true}` and `DELETE /v1/tasks/77`.

**Assert.** Each must be refused. TaskFlow's documented choice is **404 Not Found**, which hides that task 77 exists (unit 9 explains why some APIs use 403 instead). The test asserts that exact code. It must never be `200` or `204`, and the GET body must not contain Bob's title.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5; OWASP Web Security Testing Guide — Insecure Direct Object References, WSTG-ATHZ-04 (https://wstg.owasp.org/latest/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/05-Authorization/04-Insecure_Direct_Object_References), CC BY-SA 4.0. Reference (not copied): Ham Vocke, The Practical Test Pyramid (https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html).

chunks.section: Checking side effects: Bob's task is unchanged
chunks.text:
Testing Your API — Checking side effects: Bob's task is unchanged

A refusal status is not enough. A buggy handler could write to the database first and only then return 403. So after Alice's PATCH and DELETE attempts, assert directly on Bob's row:

```sql
SELECT owner_id, title, done FROM tasks WHERE id = 77;
```

```text
assert row exists                       -- DELETE did not remove it
assert row.owner_id == 456              -- still Bob's
assert row.title == "Bob's secret plan"
assert row.done == false                -- PATCH did not apply
```

Then the positive control: with **Bob's** token, `GET /v1/tasks/77` returns `200` and his title. This proves the 404/403 for Alice was due to authorization, not because the task was missing or the test was set up wrongly.

Also test the list: `GET /v1/tasks` with Alice's token must not include task 77. Leaks through list endpoints are a common IDOR variant.

Reference (not copied): Ham Vocke, The Practical Test Pyramid (https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html).

chunks.text:
Testing Your API — Test data and isolation

Each test must be **independent**: it creates the data it needs, and its result does not depend on which tests ran before it or in what order.

Bad: test A creates Alice's task; test B assumes the task exists. Run B alone, or in a different order, and it fails for no real reason. Tests that pass or fail depending on order are called **flaky**, and teams soon stop trusting them.

Practical habits:

- **Fresh data per test**: start each test from an empty test database, or wrap each test in a transaction that is rolled back afterwards.
- **Arrange explicitly**: create Alice, Bob and their tasks inside the test, so a reader sees everything that matters.
- **Never use production data**. Use a separate test database with fake users like `alice@example.com`.
- **Avoid hidden time dependence**: "due date in the future" should be computed from a controlled "today", not a hard-coded date that expires next year.

chunks.section: Worked example: a test plan for PUT /tasks/{id}
chunks.text:
Testing Your API — Worked example: a test plan for PUT /tasks/{id}

Before writing code, list the cases. `PUT` **replaces** the whole task, so `title`, `done` and `due_date` must all be sent. Arrange for every row: Alice (123) owns task 42; Bob (456) owns task 77.

| # | Case | Request | Expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Happy path | Alice, PUT 42, all valid fields | 200, body matches, row updated |
| 2 | Idempotent | same PUT sent twice | 200 both times, same row |
| 3 | Missing field | body without `title` | 422, row unchanged |
| 4 | Max title | 200-char title | 200 |
| 5 | Over max | 201-char title | 422, row unchanged |
| 6 | Bad type | `"done": "yes"` | 422 |
| 7 | Past date | `due_date` yesterday | 422 |
| 8 | Malformed | `{"title": "x",` | 400 |

Note how "row unchanged" appears on failure rows: a rejected PUT must not partly apply.

Reference (not copied): Ham Vocke, The Practical Test Pyramid (https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html).

chunks.text:
Testing Your API — Test plan for PUT /tasks/{id}, continued

The remaining rows cover resources, identity and permission:

| # | Case | Request | Expect |
|---|---|---|---|
| 9 | Not found | Alice, PUT 999999 | 404, no row created |
| 10 | No token | PUT 42, no `Authorization` | 401, row unchanged |
| 11 | Expired token | Alice's expired token | 401, row unchanged |
| 12 | Other user | Alice's token, PUT 77 | 404 (TaskFlow hides other users' tasks), Bob's row unchanged |
| 13 | Owner swap | Alice, PUT 42 with `"owner_id": 456` | 422, owner still 123 |
| 14 | Wrong media type | `Content-Type: text/plain` | 415 |
| 15 | Control | Bob's token, PUT 77 | 200 |

Fifteen tests for one endpoint, and only two are happy paths (rows 1 and 15). That ratio is normal. Each row becomes one independent arrange–act–assert test.

chunks.text:
Testing Your API — Common mistakes

**Mistake: asserting only the status code.** Why wrong: a `201` with the wrong `owner_id` saved still passes. Correct: also check the body and the database row.

**Mistake: testing only the happy path.** Why wrong: most bugs and all attacks are in failure cases. Correct: several failure tests per endpoint, including boundaries and auth.

**Mistake: testing authorization with one user.** Why wrong: you cannot detect IDOR without a second user's object. Correct: Alice and Bob, swap ids, and check Bob's row afterwards.

**Mistake: tests that depend on each other.** Why wrong: order changes make them fail randomly. Correct: each test arranges its own data from a clean state.

**Mistake: only testing invalid values far from the limit** (e.g. a 5,000-character title). Why wrong: off-by-one bugs live at the edge. Correct: test 200 and 201.

**Mistake: mostly E2E browser tests.** Correct: many unit tests, fewer integration tests, a handful of E2E.

Reference (not copied): Ham Vocke, The Practical Test Pyramid (https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html).

chunks.text:
Testing Your API — Summary

- Tests catch regressions and document behaviour; "it worked in the browser" proves one case once.
- Assert four things: status, body, headers, and database side effects.
- Most bugs hide in failure cases; write several per happy path.
- Unit tests check small logic in isolation; integration tests check real HTTP plus a real database; E2E tests drive the whole system. Use the pyramid: many unit, some integration, few E2E.
- Structure every test as arrange–act–assert, one behaviour per test.
- Test validation at the boundaries (1, 200, 201 characters) and confirm rejected requests write nothing.
- Test 404 for missing ids on every method; empty lists stay 200 `[]`.
- No token or expired token → 401.
- Authorization: two users, swap ids; expect 403/404 on GET, PATCH, DELETE and verify the other user's row is unchanged.
- Each test sets up its own data; no order dependence.

chunks.section: Exercise: Find the gaps in a test suite
chunks.text:
Testing Your API — Exercise: Find the gaps in a test suite

A teammate's entire test suite for `DELETE /tasks/{id}` is one test: it creates Alice (user 123) and her task 42, sends `DELETE /v1/tasks/42` with Alice's token, and asserts that the status is `204`. They say the endpoint is "fully tested".

Explain why this is not enough. List at least five additional tests you would add (covering side effects, missing resources, authentication and authorization), and for each give the arrange step, the request, and the expected status plus any database check. Explain why one of your tests needs Bob (user 456).

chunks.text:
Authentication: Who Are You? — Why this matters

Think of an office building. At the entrance you show ID and receive a badge. The badge proves **who you are**. Separately, each door has rules about whose badge opens it: everyone may enter the lobby, only the finance team may enter the finance room. Those door rules decide **which rooms you may enter**.

Before TaskFlow can show Alice "her" tasks, it must be sure the request really comes from Alice. If that step is weak, nothing built on it can be trusted.

This unit covers the badge: **authentication**. The next unit, Authorization, covers the door rules. They work together but answer different questions.

chunks.text:
Authentication: Who Are You? — Authentication vs authorization

Two words that sound alike and are constantly confused:

- **Authentication (authn)** — proving *who* is making the request. "This request comes from user 123, Alice."
- **Authorization (authz)** — deciding *what* that identity is allowed to do. "User 123 may read task 42 because she owns it."

Authentication always comes first: you cannot decide what someone may do until you know who they are. A request can pass authentication and still fail authorization (Alice is really Alice, but task 77 belongs to Bob).

**Credentials** are the things a client presents to prove identity: an email + password at login, and afterwards a session cookie or a token on each request.

HTTP status codes follow the same split. **401 Unauthorized** means "I don't know who you are" (an authentication problem, despite the name). **403 Forbidden** means "I know who you are, and you may not do this" (an authorization problem, covered in the next unit).

chunks.section: Worked example: Logging in with a session cookie
chunks.text:
Authentication: Who Are You? — Worked example: Logging in with a session cookie

Alice opens the TaskFlow web app and types her email and password. The app sends them in the request **body** of `POST /login`, never in the URL:

```http
POST /v1/login HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Content-Type: application/json

{"email": "alice@example.com", "password": "correct horse battery"}
```

The server looks up the user by email, checks the password against the stored hash, and creates a **session**: a random ID it remembers on its side. It hands the ID to the browser in a cookie:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Set-Cookie: __Host-tf_session=Gk3vQ9xL2pR7mWz8aT1yB4nC; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Max-Age=1800
Content-Type: application/json

{"user": {"id": 123, "name": "Alice"}}
```

Step by step: `Secure` means the cookie only travels over HTTPS; `HttpOnly` means page JavaScript cannot read it; `SameSite=Strict` stops it being sent on requests started by other sites; `Max-Age=1800` makes it expire after 30 minutes. The browser now stores the cookie and attaches it automatically from here on.

chunks.section: Worked example: Logging in with a token
chunks.text:
Authentication: Who Are You? — Worked example: Logging in with a token

A mobile app or a script often prefers a **token** instead of a cookie. The login request is identical; the response differs:

```http
POST /v1/login HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Content-Type: application/json

{"email": "alice@example.com", "password": "correct horse battery"}

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
Cache-Control: no-store

{
  "access_token": "eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiIxMjMi...",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 3600
}
```

The client must keep this string and attach it to every later request itself. `expires_in: 3600` = valid for one hour. `Cache-Control: no-store` asks caches not to keep this credential-bearing response.

The same curl call from a terminal:

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.taskflow.example/v1/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"alice@example.com","password":"correct horse battery"}'
```

chunks.text:
Authentication: Who Are You? — Sending credentials on every request

HTTP is **stateless**: each request stands alone, and the server does not "remember" that Alice logged in a minute ago on the same connection. So the client must prove its identity on **every** request after login. There are two common places to put the credential.

With a session cookie, the browser adds a `Cookie` header automatically:

```http
GET /v1/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Cookie: __Host-tf_session=Gk3vQ9xL2pR7mWz8aT1yB4nC
```

With a token, the client adds an `Authorization` header using the `Bearer` scheme ("whoever bears this token is the user"):

```http
GET /v1/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9...
```

Either way, the server works out "this is user 123" before handling the request. General format: `Authorization: <scheme> <credentials>`.

chunks.text:
Authentication: Who Are You? — Sessions: the server remembers

With **sessions**, the server keeps a record and the client holds only a meaningless key to it.

What the server stores (for example in a `sessions` table or a fast store such as Redis):

```sql
-- id is the random value sent in the cookie
SELECT user_id, expires_at FROM sessions
WHERE id = 'Gk3vQ9xL2pR7mWz8aT1yB4nC';
-- user_id = 123, expires_at = 2026-10-14 10:30:00+00
```

How each request is checked: read the cookie, look up the session ID, reject it if it is missing or past `expires_at`, otherwise treat the request as user 123.

Rules from OWASP: the session ID must be random and unguessable (at least 64 bits of entropy from a cryptographically secure generator) and must contain no personal data; issue a **new** session ID at login (so an attacker cannot plant one in advance, called session fixation); and on logout **delete the session on the server**, not just the cookie in the browser. Because the server holds the record, it can end a session instantly.

chunks.text:
Authentication: Who Are You? — Tokens: the server verifies

With a **self-contained token** such as a JWT, the token itself carries the facts ("user 123, expires at 10:20") plus a **signature** that only the server can produce. The server does not need to look anything up; it checks the token mathematically.

How each request is checked:

1. Read the `Authorization: Bearer ...` header.
2. Verify the signature with the server's secret key. If anyone changed even one character, verification fails.
3. Check the expiry time (`exp`). If it is in the past, reject.
4. Read the user ID from the token (`sub: "123"`).

What the server stores: only its signing key, no record per login. The catch: a valid token keeps working until it expires, even after "log out", unless the server adds a deny-list. So access tokens are usually **short-lived** (minutes to an hour).

Not every token is self-contained: some are just random strings that the server looks up, which behaves like a session.

chunks.section: Sessions vs tokens: expiry and logout
chunks.text:
Authentication: Who Are You? — Sessions vs tokens: expiry and logout

| | Session cookie | Self-contained token (JWT) |
|---|---|---|
| Client holds | random session ID | signed token with claims |
| Server stores | a session record per login | only its signing key |
| Checked by | lookup in session store | signature + `exp` check |
| Sent in | `Cookie` header (automatic) | `Authorization: Bearer` (by the app) |
| Logout | delete the record: works instantly | token stays valid until `exp` |

Both must **expire**. OWASP recommends two timeouts for sessions, enforced on the server: an **idle timeout** (for example 15–30 minutes of no activity for a low-risk app) and an **absolute timeout** (for example 4–8 hours, however active the user is). For tokens the expiry is written inside the token.

Neither is "the secure one"; both are fine when done properly.

chunks.text:
Authentication: Who Are You? — What a JWT is

A **JSON Web Token (JWT)**, pronounced "jot", is a token made of three Base64URL-encoded parts joined by dots: `header.payload.signature`. Here is a real one for Alice:

```text
eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9
.eyJzdWIiOiIxMjMiLCJuYW1lIjoiQWxpY2UiLCJpYXQiOjE3NjA0MzAwMDAsImV4cCI6MTc2MDQzMzYwMH0
.7yVeawaWH1Jsrl-Dj4ZG7blUxOQaA4sAueNx_kDA2E8
```

(Line breaks added for reading; the real token is one line.) Decoded:

```json
{"alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT"}
{"sub": "123", "name": "Alice", "iat": 1760430000, "exp": 1760433600}
```

- **Header** — which algorithm signed it (`HS256` = HMAC with SHA-256).
- **Payload** — the **claims**: `sub` (subject, the user ID), `iat` (issued at) and `exp` (expires at), as Unix timestamps.
- **Signature** — computed from header + payload with the server's secret key. It proves the server issued the token and nobody edited it.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — HTTP authentication (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Authentication), Using HTTP cookies (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Cookies), 401 Unauthorized (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/401), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5; OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — Authentication (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html), Password Storage (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html), Session Management (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html), CC BY-SA 4.0

chunks.text:
Authentication: Who Are You? — JWTs are signed, not encrypted

The most important fact about a JWT: **anyone can read the payload.** Base64URL is an encoding, not encryption. Paste a JWT into any decoder and the claims appear in plain text.

The signature gives **integrity**, not secrecy. If Alice edits her payload to say `"sub": "456"` hoping to become Bob, the signature no longer matches and the server rejects the token. But she can still *read* everything inside.

Consequences:

- **Never put secrets in a JWT**: no passwords, no password hashes, no API keys, no private personal data.
- Put only what the server needs to identify the user: an ID, an expiry, perhaps a role.
- The server must actually **verify** the signature and the `exp` claim on every request; decoding without verifying is the same as trusting whatever the client wrote.
- A JWT is still a credential: whoever steals it can act as Alice until it expires.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — HTTP authentication (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Authentication), Using HTTP cookies (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Cookies), 401 Unauthorized (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/401), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5; OWASP Cheat Sheet Series — Authentication (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html), Password Storage (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html), Session Management (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html), CC BY-SA 4.0

chunks.text:
Authentication: Who Are You? — Storing passwords: never plain text

The server must **never** store the password itself (plain text), nor encrypt it (whoever gets the key gets every password).

Instead, store a **password hash**: the output of a one-way function. At login, hash what the user typed and compare. A stolen hash cannot be turned back into the password.

Two extra ingredients matter:

- **Salt** — a random value, unique per user, mixed in before hashing. Two users with the same password get different hashes, and precomputed "rainbow tables" become useless.
- **Slowness** — fast hashes (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256) let an attacker with a GPU try billions of guesses per second against a stolen database. Password hashing algorithms are deliberately **slow** (and Argon2id is also memory-hard).

OWASP's recommendation: **Argon2id** (minimum m=19 MiB memory, t=2 iterations, p=1); scrypt if Argon2id is unavailable; **bcrypt** for legacy systems with a work factor of at least 10 (and note bcrypt only uses the first 72 bytes of the password).

chunks.section: Worked example: What the users table stores
chunks.text:
Authentication: Who Are You? — Worked example: What the users table stores

Alice signs up with the password `correct horse battery`. Here is what the `users` table should and should not hold.

Wrong (plain text — one database leak exposes every password):

```text
 id  | email             | password
 123 | alice@example.com | correct horse battery
```

Also wrong (fast, unsalted SHA-256 — same password, same hash; guessing is cheap):

```text
 123 | alice@example.com | 9028ea0d15decaa35b2da21c0290af3b1a5ba0a30a591906f89b5074e209ea72
```

Right (Argon2id in the standard "PHC string" format; values shortened):

```text
 id  | email             | password_hash
 123 | alice@example.com | $argon2id$v=19$m=19456,t=2,p=1$c2FsdHlTYWx0MTIz$Jx9k...Qw
```

Left to right: algorithm, version, cost parameters (memory, iterations, parallelism), the **salt**, then the hash. Keeping the parameters in the string lets the server raise the cost later and re-hash at the user's next login. At login it hashes the typed password with that salt and those parameters and compares.

chunks.text:
Authentication: Who Are You? — 401 Unauthorized and WWW-Authenticate

**401 Unauthorized** means: this request does not carry **valid authentication credentials**. Despite its name it is about authentication ("who are you?"), not permission. Typical causes on TaskFlow:

- **Missing** — no `Cookie` or `Authorization` header at all.
- **Invalid** — the token's signature is wrong, the session ID is unknown, or the login password was wrong.
- **Expired** — the token's `exp` has passed or the session timed out.

A 401 tells the client "authenticate (again) and retry", which might succeed. Contrast with 403, where re-authenticating changes nothing.

The HTTP standard says a 401 response carries a **`WWW-Authenticate`** header naming the scheme the server expects, so the client knows how to retry:

```http
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="taskflow"
```

For Bearer tokens, the header may add an `error` such as `invalid_token` with a short description. Keep descriptions brief and never echo the token back.

chunks.section: Worked example: Missing, invalid and expired credentials
chunks.text:
Authentication: Who Are You? — Worked example: Missing, invalid and expired credentials

Three failed requests to the same endpoint, each answered 401.

1) No credentials at all:

```http
GET /v1/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example

HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="taskflow"
Content-Type: application/json

{"error": "authentication_required"}
```

2) Tampered token (someone edited the payload, so the signature fails):

```http
GET /v1/tasks HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9.eyJzdWIiOiI0NTYifQ.7yVeaw...

HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="taskflow", error="invalid_token"
```

3) Token past its `exp` (issued 09:20, valid one hour, now 10:45):

```http
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="taskflow", error="invalid_token", error_description="token expired"
```

In every case the server does **not** run the handler or return partial data. The client's fix is the same: log in again (or refresh the token) and retry.

chunks.text:
Authentication: Who Are You? — HTTPS is required

Everything in this unit assumes **HTTPS** (HTTP over TLS). Without it, every byte travels in readable form across Wi-Fi networks, routers and proxies:

- The `POST /login` body exposes Alice's password.
- The `Cookie` or `Authorization` header exposes her session or token, and anyone who copies it **is** Alice until it expires (session hijacking).

OWASP: the login page and all authenticated pages must be served exclusively over TLS. In practice for an API:

- Serve `https://api.taskflow.example` only; refuse or redirect plain `http://` before any credential is sent.
- Mark session cookies `Secure` so the browser never sends them over plain HTTP.
- Remember that Basic authentication and Base64 are encodings, not protection: `Basic YWxpY2U6c2VjcmV0` decodes instantly to `alice:secret`.

HTTPS protects credentials **in transit**; it does not replace password hashing (**at rest**).

chunks.section: Common mistakes: Credentials in URLs and browser storage
chunks.text:
Authentication: Who Are You? — Common mistakes: Credentials in URLs and browser storage

**Mistake: passwords or tokens in the URL.** `GET /v1/login?email=alice@example.com&password=correct+horse+battery` or `GET /v1/tasks?token=eyJ...`. *Why it's wrong:* URLs end up in server and proxy logs, browser history and bookmarks; HTTPS does not hide them there. *Correct:* send the password in the body of `POST /login`; send tokens in the `Authorization` header.

**Mistake: storing tokens in `localStorage` without thinking about XSS.** *Why it's risky:* any JavaScript running on the page can read `localStorage`. If an attacker manages to inject a script (a cross-site scripting bug), they can copy the token and use it elsewhere. OWASP advises against keeping session IDs or tokens in web storage. *Correct (careful version):* for browser apps, prefer an `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite` session cookie, which scripts cannot read. Cookies bring their own concern (cross-site request forgery), handled by `SameSite` and CSRF protections; preventing XSS matters either way.

chunks.section: Common mistakes: Login errors that leak information
chunks.text:
Authentication: Who Are You? — Common mistakes: Login errors that leak information

**Mistake: different answers for "unknown email" and "wrong password".**

```json
{"error": "No account with email bob@example.com"}
{"error": "Wrong password for bob@example.com"}
```

*Why it's wrong:* an attacker can now test a list of emails and learn which ones have TaskFlow accounts (user enumeration), then focus password guessing on them. Different status codes, or a noticeably faster reply for unknown emails, leak the same fact.

*Correct:* one generic message and the same status for every failure, with similar response time:

```http
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
Content-Type: application/json

{"error": "invalid_credentials", "message": "Invalid email or password."}
```

The same idea applies to password reset: "If that email address is registered, we have sent a reset link."

**Mistake: unlimited login attempts.** *Correct:* limit failed attempts per account, slow down repeated failures, and offer multi-factor authentication (OWASP calls MFA by far the best defence against most password attacks).

chunks.text:
Authentication: Who Are You? — Summary

- **Authentication** proves who you are (the badge); **authorization** decides what you may do (the door rules). Authentication comes first; this unit is that first half.
- Log in with `POST /login`, credentials in the JSON **body**; the server answers with a session cookie or a token.
- HTTP is stateless, so send the credential on **every** request: `Cookie:` header or `Authorization: Bearer`.
- **Sessions**: server stores a record, client holds a random ID, logout deletes the record. **Tokens**: server verifies a signature and `exp`, stores no per-login record, so keep them short-lived.
- A **JWT** is `header.payload.signature`: signed, **not** encrypted. Anyone can read it; never put secrets in it; always verify it.
- Store passwords as **slow, salted hashes** (Argon2id, or bcrypt for legacy), never plain text or fast SHA-256/MD5.
- **401** = missing, invalid or expired credentials, sent with `WWW-Authenticate`.
- Use **HTTPS** everywhere; keep credentials out of URLs; prefer `HttpOnly` cookies in browsers; give one generic login error.

chunks.section: Exercise: Review the TaskFlow login design
chunks.text:
Authentication: Who Are You? — Exercise: Review the TaskFlow login design

A new teammate proposes this design for TaskFlow and asks for your review:

1. Users log in with `GET /v1/login?email=...&password=...`.
2. Passwords are stored in the `users` table as unsalted SHA-256 hashes "because SHA-256 is secure".
3. A wrong password returns `404 {"error": "email not found"}` or `401 {"error": "wrong password"}` depending on the case.
4. After login the server returns a JWT whose payload contains `{"sub": "123", "email": "alice@example.com", "password_hash": "..."}` and which never expires.

For each of the four points, explain what is wrong and why, and describe the corrected version (method and where credentials go, how passwords are stored, what the error response looks like, and what the token should contain).

chunks.text:
Authentication: Who Are You? — Exercise: Sessions or tokens after logout

Alice logs in to TaskFlow on a library computer, then clicks "Log out" and leaves. Ten minutes later, someone else uses a copy of the credential her browser sent.

Compare two versions of TaskFlow: (a) one that uses a server-side session in an `HttpOnly; Secure` cookie, and (b) one that uses a JWT valid for 24 hours. For each, explain what the server stores, how it checks the copied credential, and whether the attacker's request `GET /v1/tasks` succeeds or receives `401 Unauthorized`. Then recommend one change that would reduce the risk in version (b).

chunks.text:
Authorization: What May You Do? — Why this matters

Back in the office building: at the entrance you got a badge that proves who you are. That was authentication. Now imagine the building **never checks the badge at individual doors**. Anyone with *any* badge can walk into the finance room, the server room, or the CEO's office. The badge is real; the security is still broken.

That is the most common serious flaw in real APIs, ranked **number one** in the OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023): the login works, the token is valid, yet one user can read, change or delete another user's data by changing a number in the URL.

Authorization is the set of **door rules**. Authentication tells TaskFlow "this is Alice"; authorization decides "Alice may read task 42, but not task 77, and she may not open the admin panel". This unit shows how the flaw happens, why popular quick fixes don't work, and how to write the check correctly.

chunks.text:
Authorization: What May You Do? — What authorization means

**Authorization** is the decision, made **on the server**, on **every request**, about whether **this** authenticated user may perform **this** action on **this** resource.

Each part matters:

- **This user** — the identity comes from the verified session or token (the previous unit), never from something the client typed into the URL or body.
- **This action** — reading is not the same as editing or deleting. `GET`, `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` each need a decision.
- **This resource** — not "tasks in general" but *task 77* specifically, with its own owner.
- **Every request** — being allowed yesterday, or on the previous request, proves nothing about this one.
- **On the server** — the only place the user cannot tamper with.

Mental test: *"If I were logged in as Bob and replayed Alice's request, what would stop me?"* If "nothing", there is no authorization.

chunks.text:
Authorization: What May You Do? — Never trust the client

The TaskFlow web app only shows Alice a "Delete" button on her own tasks, and it never shows the "Admin" menu to normal users. That is good **user experience**, but it is **not security**.

Why: the client is fully under the user's control. Alice can open her browser's developer tools, copy any request as curl, edit the URL, method, headers and body, and send it directly:

```bash
curl -X DELETE https://api.taskflow.example/v1/tasks/77 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9..."
```

OWASP's rule: **developers must never rely on client-side access control checks.** Hidden buttons, disabled form fields, greyed-out menus and JavaScript `if (user.isAdmin)` checks are all decoration. The real decision must happen in server code that runs for every request, whatever sent it.

chunks.text:
Authorization: What May You Do? — Deny by default

**Deny by default** means: unless a rule explicitly grants access, the answer is no.

Compare two ways to write the same rule in pseudocode:

```text
# Allow by default (fragile)
if user.role == "banned": deny()
allow()

# Deny by default (safe)
if task.owner_id == current_user.id: allow()
if current_user.role == "admin": allow()
deny()
```

With allow-by-default, every case you *forgot* (a new role, a null owner, a new endpoint) is silently allowed. With deny-by-default, forgotten cases fail closed: an annoying but safe and visible error.

The same applies to whole endpoints. When a developer adds `DELETE /v1/tasks/{id}` next week, it should start out requiring a permission check, not start out open. OWASP: an attacker only needs to find **one** way in, so checks must be applied consistently and globally, not on "most" requests.

chunks.section: Worked example: Alice opens her own task list
chunks.text:
Authorization: What May You Do? — Worked example: Alice opens her own task list

Suppose TaskFlow has added an endpoint to list a given user's tasks, `GET /v1/users/{id}/tasks`. Alice (user 123) is logged in, and her app requests her list:

```http
GET /v1/users/123/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiIxMjMi...

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

[
  {"id": 42, "owner_id": 123, "title": "Buy milk", "done": false},
  {"id": 43, "owner_id": 123, "title": "Book dentist", "done": true}
]
```

Everything looks correct: the token is valid and Alice sees her two tasks. A tester clicking through the app finds no problem.

Here is the handler the developer wrote:

```text
handle GET /v1/users/{id}/tasks:
    user = authenticate(request)          # 401 if token missing/invalid
    tasks = db.query("SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE owner_id = $1", path.id)
    return 200, tasks
```

`authenticate` returns `user.id = 123`, but the query **never uses it**. It uses `path.id`, from the URL the client chose.

chunks.text:
Authorization: What May You Do? — Worked example: Alice changes 123 to 456

Alice is curious. She edits one number in the URL and sends the request again with **her own, perfectly valid token**:

```http
GET /v1/users/456/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiIxMjMi...

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

[
  {"id": 77, "owner_id": 456, "title": "Prepare salary negotiation", "done": false},
  {"id": 78, "owner_id": 456, "title": "Doctor: test results", "done": false}
]
```

She receives **Bob's** private tasks. Step by step:

1. Authentication succeeded: the token really is Alice's (`sub: "123"`).
2. The handler ran `SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE owner_id = 456` because 456 was in the path.
3. Nothing compared "who is asking" (123) with "whose data this is" (456).

No password was stolen and no token forged. A loop from 1 to 100000 would download every user's tasks in minutes.

chunks.text:
Authorization: What May You Do? — Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA / IDOR)

What happened to Bob has a name: **Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA)**, **API1:2023** in the OWASP API Security Top 10. The older, equivalent name is **Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR)**.

Definition: an API accepts an **object identifier** from the client (path, query, headers or body) and acts on that object **without checking that the logged-in user may act on it**. Three ingredients: an object, a reference to it, and a missing check.

Real cases from OWASP's descriptions:

- A shop platform served `/shops/{shopName}/revenue_data.json`; an attacker listed shop names and scripted requests for thousands of stores' sales.
- A car maker's API unlocked doors and started engines by Vehicle Identification Number without checking the VIN belonged to the caller.
- A document service deleted any document by ID with no further permission check.

Consequences: data disclosure, loss or manipulation, sometimes account takeover. "Object level" = the check concerns one specific record.

chunks.section: Misconception: hide or randomise the ID
chunks.text:
Authorization: What May You Do? — Misconception: hide or randomise the ID

A common first reaction: "Let's make IDs hard to find." Variants: don't show IDs in the UI, use UUIDs like `/v1/tasks/9f1c2e7a-4b3d-4e8a-a6f2-0c5d7b1e9a34` instead of `/v1/tasks/77`, or "encrypt" the ID in the URL. None of these is access control.

Why hiding fails: IDs **leak**. They appear in shared links, emails and notifications, browser history, server and proxy logs, screenshots posted in support chats, other API responses (a task's `owner_id`, a list of team members), and the app's own network traffic, which any user can inspect.

Why randomising is not enough: a UUID makes **guessing** much harder, so OWASP recommends random, unpredictable IDs as **defence in depth**. But the moment an attacker *obtains* the ID by any route above, the request succeeds, because the server still never asks "is this yours?". OWASP's IDOR cheat sheet is explicit: access control is crucial even with complex identifiers.

Rule: an ID says **which** object. Only a server-side permission check says **whether you may** touch it.

chunks.section: Writing the check: load, then compare
chunks.text:
Authorization: What May You Do? — Writing the check: load, then compare

Compare **the identity from the verified token** with **the owner stored in the database**, on every request. Approach one: load, then check.

```text
handle GET /v1/tasks/{id}:
    user = authenticate(request)               # from session/token, 401 if invalid
    task = db.query_one("SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE id = $1", path.id)
    if task is null:
        return 404
    if task.owner_id != user.id:               # the authorization check
        return 404                              # or 403, see below
    return 200, task
```

For the list endpoint, the resource is "user {id}'s task list", so compare the path with the authenticated identity:

```text
handle GET /v1/users/{id}/tasks:
    user = authenticate(request)
    if path.id != user.id and user.role != "admin":
        return 403
    return 200, db.query("SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE owner_id = $1", user.id)
```

`user.id` comes from the verified token or session record. Client-chosen values (`path.id`, body fields, an `X-User-Id` header) never decide the answer.

chunks.section: Writing the check: scope the query
chunks.text:
Authorization: What May You Do? — Writing the check: scope the query

A second approach, often safer, puts the ownership condition **inside the database query**, so a lookup for someone else's task simply finds nothing:

```sql
SELECT id, title, done, due_date
FROM tasks
WHERE id = $1          -- task id from the URL
  AND owner_id = $2;   -- user id from the verified token
```

```text
handle GET /v1/tasks/{id}:
    user = authenticate(request)
    task = db.query_one(
        "SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2",
        path.id, user.id)
    if task is null:
        return 404       # doesn't exist OR isn't yours: same answer
    return 200, task
```

No separate `if` to forget, and the same pattern works for `UPDATE` and `DELETE`. OWASP calls this **scoping lookups to the current user**. The `$1`, `$2` parameters keep values separate from the SQL text, as in the queries-safety unit, so it is also injection-safe.

The flat `GET /v1/tasks` does the same: user from the token, no user ID in the URL to tamper with.

chunks.text:
Authorization: What May You Do? — Worked example: The fixed /users/456/tasks request

After the fix, Alice repeats the attack:

```http
GET /v1/users/456/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiIxMjMi...

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/json

{"error": "forbidden", "message": "You do not have access to this resource."}
```

And for a single task of Bob's, using the scoped query:

```http
GET /v1/tasks/77 HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiIxMjMi...

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/json

{"error": "not_found", "message": "Task not found."}
```

Her own request `GET /v1/users/123/tasks` still returns `200 OK` with tasks 42 and 43. Step by step: authentication still says 123; the server compares 123 with 456 (or with task 77's `owner_id` 456); they differ; the request is refused **before** any of Bob's data is read or returned. The error body names no titles, owners or other details.

chunks.text:
Authorization: What May You Do? — 403 or 404 for someone else's resource

When Alice asks for Bob's task, two answers are both widely used and both acceptable:

- **403 Forbidden** — "I know who you are, the resource exists, and you may not access it." Re-authenticating will not help (that is the difference from 401). It is honest and helps debugging, but it confirms that task 77 exists.
- **404 Not Found** — "As far as you are concerned, there is no such task." MDN and OWASP both note that servers may return 404 instead of 403 to **hide the existence** of a resource from users without access. The scoped query produces this naturally.

Guidance for TaskFlow: use **404** for individual private objects (`/v1/tasks/77`), so outsiders cannot even map which IDs exist; use **403** when the resource's existence is no secret but the action is off-limits, such as a normal user calling an admin endpoint. Whatever you choose, be **consistent**, and never return 200 with an empty or partial body for a forbidden object.

Quick map: **401** = who are you? **403** = I know you; no. **404** = nothing here for you.

chunks.section: Worked example: Bob's task via PUT, PATCH and DELETE
chunks.text:
Authorization: What May You Do? — Worked example: Bob's task via PUT, PATCH and DELETE

A developer fixes `GET /v1/tasks/{id}` but leaves the other methods as they were. Alice tries them on Bob's task 77:

```http
PATCH /v1/tasks/77 HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer eyJ...(Alice)
Content-Type: application/json

{"done": true}

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{"id": 77, "owner_id": 456, "title": "Prepare salary negotiation", "done": true}
```

```http
DELETE /v1/tasks/77 HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer eyJ...(Alice)

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
```

Bob's task was changed, then deleted. Reading was protected; writing was not, which is arguably worse. OWASP explicitly asks: can a user perform sensitive actions just by **changing the HTTP method**?

Fix: every method on `/v1/tasks/{id}` carries the ownership condition:

```sql
UPDATE tasks SET done = $1 WHERE id = $2 AND owner_id = $3;
DELETE FROM tasks WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2;
```

If zero rows were affected, return 404. Alice's `DELETE /v1/tasks/77` now gets `404 Not Found` and Bob's task survives.

chunks.text:
Authorization: What May You Do? — Function-level authorization and roles

So far: **object-level** authorization — may this user touch *this record*? **Function-level** authorization asks: may this user call *this endpoint or operation at all*? Some functions are meant only for certain **roles**. TaskFlow, for example, has support staff with `role = "admin"` who can call `GET /v1/admin/users` (list every account) or `DELETE /v1/users/{id}`.

When a normal user can reach such a function, OWASP calls it **Broken Function Level Authorization (BFLA), API5:2023**. Examples: an unprotected `GET /api/admin/v1/users/all` leaking every user, and a user switching `GET /api/invites/{guid}` to `POST /api/invites/new` to invite themselves as admin.

Prevention, from OWASP:

- Deny all access by default; grant each function explicitly to specific roles.
- Don't rely on a URL being undocumented; attackers guess paths.
- Read the role from the **server's** records (or a server-signed token), never from a client field.

Object-level and function-level checks are independent: an endpoint can need both.

chunks.text:
Authorization: What May You Do? — Worked example: An admin-only endpoint

Alice (role `user`) notices the web app's JavaScript mentions `/v1/admin/users` and tries it. She even adds a header she hopes will help:

```http
GET /v1/admin/users HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Authorization: Bearer eyJ...(Alice, sub 123)
X-Role: admin

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/json

{"error": "forbidden", "message": "This action requires the admin role."}
```

Step by step on the server:

```text
handle GET /v1/admin/users:
    user = authenticate(request)            # 401 if no valid token
    role = db.query_one("SELECT role FROM users WHERE id = $1", user.id)
    if role != "admin":                     # deny by default
        return 403
    return 200, db.query("SELECT id, email, name FROM users")
```

The `X-Role` header is ignored: the role comes from the database row for user 123. 403 fits here because the endpoint's existence is no secret; the point is that Alice's role is not allowed. Note that even the admin response leaves out `password_hash`.

chunks.section: Worked example: Alice sends owner_id in a PATCH
chunks.text:
Authorization: What May You Do? — Worked example: Alice sends owner_id in a PATCH

A subtler attack: Alice edits her **own** task, but adds a field the app never sends:

```http
PATCH /v1/tasks/42 HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer eyJ...(Alice)
Content-Type: application/json

{"title": "Buy milk", "owner_id": 456}
```

If the server copies every body field into the row (**mass assignment**), task 42 now belongs to Bob. The ownership check passed for the row she addressed, but she rewrote the very field the check depends on.

Fix: decide on the server which fields a client may change, and ignore or reject everything else.

```text
allowed = {"title", "done", "due_date"}
if any key in body not in allowed:
    return 400 {"error": "unknown_or_readonly_field", "field": "owner_id"}
UPDATE tasks SET title = $1 WHERE id = $2 AND owner_id = $3
```

On `POST /v1/tasks`, likewise, set `owner_id` from the token, never from the body. Fields like `owner_id`, `id`, `role` and `created_at` are server-controlled.

chunks.text:
Authorization: What May You Do? — Common mistakes

- **Trusting a user ID the client sends.** `GET /v1/tasks?user_id=123` or a header `X-User-Id: 123`. *Why wrong:* the client can send 456. *Correct:* take the identity only from the verified session or token.
- **"It's authenticated, so it's safe."** *Why wrong:* BOLA happens to logged-in users with valid tokens. *Correct:* authentication and an ownership/role check, on each request.
- **Protecting GET only.** *Correct:* check `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` (and `POST` to nested resources) the same way.
- **Hiding buttons, IDs or admin URLs instead of checking.** *Correct:* UI hiding and random IDs are extras; the server check is the control.
- **Checking in some handlers only.** *Correct:* one shared check or scoped query everywhere, plus tests that log in as Bob and try Alice's endpoints; don't ship if they fail.
- **Leaky errors.** `403 {"message": "Task 77 belongs to bob@example.com"}`. *Correct:* say only that access is denied or the item is not found.

chunks.text:
Authorization: What May You Do? — Summary

- **Authorization** = on the server, on every request, may **this** user do **this** action on **this** resource? It comes after authentication.
- **Never trust the client**: hidden buttons and client-side checks are UX, not security. **Deny by default.**
- The demo story: Alice (123) changes `/v1/users/123/tasks` to `/v1/users/456/tasks` and gets Bob's tasks with her own valid token. That is **BOLA** (OWASP **API1:2023**), also called **IDOR**.
- Hiding or randomising IDs is not access control: IDs leak; UUIDs only make guessing harder.
- Fix: compare `owner_id` with the authenticated user's id, or scope the query: `WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2`.
- Someone else's object: **404** hides existence, **403** says "not allowed"; both are used. **401** is for missing or invalid credentials.
- Check **every method**, not just GET.
- **Function-level** authorization (OWASP **API5:2023**): admin-only endpoints need role checks from server-side data.
- **Mass assignment**: never accept `owner_id`, `role` or `id` from a request body.

chunks.text:
Authorization: What May You Do? — Exercise: Investigate the task-sharing bug report

A TaskFlow user reports: "I copied the link to my task, `https://app.taskflow.example/tasks/77`, into a group chat. Someone in the chat opened it while logged in as themselves and could edit and delete my task."

The API handler for task 77 currently looks like this:

```text
handle PATCH /v1/tasks/{id}:
    user = authenticate(request)
    db.execute("UPDATE tasks SET title = $1, done = $2, owner_id = $3 WHERE id = $4",
               body.title, body.done, body.owner_id, path.id)
    return 200
```

Explain (1) what kind of vulnerability this is and why the attacker did not need to guess anything, (2) at least two separate problems in this handler, and (3) the corrected handler logic, including which status code the attacker should now receive and why. Also say whether switching task IDs to UUIDs would have prevented this report.

chunks.text:
Authorization: What May You Do? — Exercise: Design the checks for a new admin feature

TaskFlow wants two new endpoints:

- `GET /v1/admin/tasks` — support staff (users with role `admin`) can list every task in the system.
- `DELETE /v1/users/{id}` — a user may delete their own account; an admin may delete any account.

For each endpoint, describe the authorization check the server must perform, where the user's identity and role come from, and which status code each of these callers receives: (a) a request with no token, (b) Alice (role `user`) calling `GET /v1/admin/tasks`, (c) Alice calling `DELETE /v1/users/456`, (d) Alice calling `DELETE /v1/users/123`, (e) an admin calling `DELETE /v1/users/456`. Name the OWASP categories the checks protect against.

chunks.text:
Tables and CRUD — Why this matters

Imagine a waiter who memorises every order but never writes anything down. When the shift ends, every order is gone. An API server is that waiter: anything it keeps in variables lives inside one running process, and a restart, a crash or a new deploy wipes it. If you run two copies of the server, each has its own memory and they disagree.

A database is the order book. It stores data on disk, outlives any single server process, and is shared by every copy of the server. When Alice creates the task "Buy milk" on Monday, it must still be there on Friday after three deploys. That is why almost every real API sits in front of a database.

In this unit you learn how TaskFlow's data is laid out in PostgreSQL tables, the four basic operations on stored data (CRUD), and exactly which SQL statement and which HTTP status code each TaskFlow endpoint uses.

metadata.source: Adapted from PostgreSQL Documentation — Tutorial: The SQL Language, Creating a New Table, Populating a Table With Rows, Querying a Table, Updates, Deletions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-sql.html) (PostgreSQL Licence); MDN Web Docs — CRUD (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/CRUD), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.text:
Tables and CRUD — Tables, rows and columns

A relational database such as PostgreSQL stores data in **tables**. A table holds data about one kind of thing: TaskFlow has a `users` table and a `tasks` table.

- A **column** is a named field with a fixed data type, for example `title` (text) or `done` (boolean). Every value in a column has that type.
- A **row** is one record: one value for each column. Alice's task "Buy milk" is one row in `tasks`.

You can picture a table like a spreadsheet:

```
 id | owner_id | title      | done  | due_date   | created_at
----+----------+------------+-------+------------+---------------------
 42 |      123 | Buy milk   | false | 2026-10-20 | 2026-10-14 09:00:00
 43 |      456 | Fix bike   | true  |            | 2026-10-14 09:05:00
```

Row 43 has an empty `due_date`: the value is NULL, meaning "no value". Unlike a spreadsheet, the database enforces the types: you cannot store the word "maybe" in `done`.

You talk to the database in **SQL**, a language of statements such as `CREATE TABLE`, `INSERT`, `SELECT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE`.

metadata.source: Adapted from PostgreSQL Documentation — Tutorial: The SQL Language, Creating a New Table, Populating a Table With Rows, Querying a Table, Updates, Deletions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-sql.html) (PostgreSQL Licence); MDN Web Docs — CRUD (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/CRUD), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.text:
Tables and CRUD — Data types and primary keys

Each column is declared with a **data type**. The ones TaskFlow needs:

- `bigint` / `int` — whole numbers (ids).
- `text` or `varchar(N)` — strings; `varchar(200)` allows up to 200 characters.
- `boolean` — `true` or `false`.
- `date` — a calendar date, written `'2026-10-20'` (the unambiguous YYYY-MM-DD form).
- `timestamptz` — a date and time with time zone.

A **primary key** is the column that identifies each row. In PostgreSQL a primary key is automatically both UNIQUE (no two rows share it) and NOT NULL (every row has one). A table has at most one primary key.

The primary key is what your URL points at: `GET /v1/tasks/42` means "the row in `tasks` whose primary key `id` is 42". Using `GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` lets the database pick the next id itself, so the client never invents ids.

metadata.source: Adapted from PostgreSQL Documentation — Tutorial: The SQL Language, Creating a New Table, Populating a Table With Rows, Querying a Table, Updates, Deletions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-sql.html) (PostgreSQL Licence); MDN Web Docs — CRUD (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/CRUD), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.text:
Tables and CRUD — The TaskFlow tables

Here are the two tables as `CREATE TABLE` statements. `--` starts a comment.

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
    id            bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    email         text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    password_hash text NOT NULL,     -- never the real password
    name          text NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE tasks (
    id          bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    owner_id    bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id),
    title       varchar(200) NOT NULL,
    done        boolean NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
    due_date    date,                -- may be NULL: "no due date"
    created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
```

Notes: `NOT NULL` forbids empty values; `DEFAULT` fills a column when the INSERT leaves it out, so a new task starts with `done = false` and the current time. `due_date` has no NOT NULL, so it is optional. `REFERENCES users (id)` links each task to its owner; the next unit explains that link.

metadata.source: Adapted from PostgreSQL Documentation — Tutorial: The SQL Language, Creating a New Table, Populating a Table With Rows, Querying a Table, Updates, Deletions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-sql.html) (PostgreSQL Licence); MDN Web Docs — CRUD (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/CRUD), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.text:
Tables and CRUD — CRUD and its SQL

**CRUD** stands for **Create, Read, Update, Delete**: the four basic operations on stored data. Every resource endpoint you designed in the previous unit is one of them, and each has a matching SQL statement and a usual HTTP method:

```
CRUD    | SQL                    | HTTP method
--------+------------------------+--------------------------
Create  | INSERT INTO ...        | POST
Read    | SELECT ... FROM ...    | GET
Update  | UPDATE ... SET ...     | PUT (replace), PATCH (part)
Delete  | DELETE FROM ...        | DELETE
```

The basic shapes, using the PostgreSQL tutorial's style of always listing columns explicitly:

```sql
INSERT INTO tasks (owner_id, title) VALUES (123, 'Buy milk');
SELECT id, title, done FROM tasks WHERE id = 42;
UPDATE tasks SET done = true WHERE id = 42;
DELETE FROM tasks WHERE id = 42;
```

The `WHERE` clause chooses which rows a statement touches. Without it, `UPDATE` changes every row and `DELETE` removes every row, with no confirmation.

metadata.source: Adapted from PostgreSQL Documentation — Tutorial: The SQL Language, Creating a New Table, Populating a Table With Rows, Querying a Table, Updates, Deletions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-sql.html) (PostgreSQL Licence); MDN Web Docs — CRUD (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/CRUD), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.text:
Tables and CRUD — Placeholders and RETURNING

In real code you never paste request values into the SQL text. You write **placeholders** `$1`, `$2`, … and send the values separately; the database treats them strictly as data. (The next unit shows the attack this prevents.)

```sql
SELECT id, title, done, due_date FROM tasks
WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2;
-- $1 = 42 (from the URL), $2 = 123 (the logged-in user)
```

`AND owner_id = $2` makes sure Alice can only see her own tasks; the next unit explains why the owner comes from the login, not from the request.

PostgreSQL's `RETURNING` clause makes `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` hand back the rows they changed, so you get the new id and default values without a second query:

```sql
INSERT INTO tasks (owner_id, title) VALUES ($1, $2)
RETURNING id, title, done, due_date, created_at;
```

The database also reports a **row count**: how many rows the statement affected. Your code uses it to decide between success and 404.

metadata.source: Adapted from PostgreSQL Documentation — Tutorial: The SQL Language, Creating a New Table, Populating a Table With Rows, Querying a Table, Updates, Deletions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-sql.html) (PostgreSQL Licence); MDN Web Docs — CRUD (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/CRUD), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.section: Worked example: POST /tasks creates a row
chunks.text:
Tables and CRUD — Worked example: POST /tasks creates a row

Alice (user 123) creates a task.

```http
POST /v1/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...
Content-Type: application/json

{"title": "Buy milk", "due_date": "2026-10-20"}
```

Step 1: validate the body (title present, date valid). Step 2: run an INSERT with the owner taken from the token:

```sql
INSERT INTO tasks (owner_id, title, due_date)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3)            -- 123, 'Buy milk', '2026-10-20'
RETURNING id, title, done, due_date, created_at;
```

Step 3: the database fills `id` (42), `done` (false) and `created_at` from the defaults and returns the row. Step 4: reply 201 Created with a Location header:

```http
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: /v1/tasks/42
Content-Type: application/json

{"id": 42, "title": "Buy milk", "done": false,
 "due_date": "2026-10-20", "created_at": "2026-10-14T09:00:00Z"}
```

metadata.source: Adapted from PostgreSQL Documentation — Tutorial: The SQL Language, Creating a New Table, Populating a Table With Rows, Querying a Table, Updates, Deletions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-sql.html) (PostgreSQL Licence); MDN Web Docs — CRUD (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/CRUD), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.section: Worked example: GET /tasks/{id} and the missing row
chunks.text:
Tables and CRUD — Worked example: GET /tasks/{id} and the missing row

Alice asks for task 42, then for task 999, which does not exist.

```http
GET /v1/tasks/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...
```

```sql
SELECT id, title, done, due_date, created_at
FROM tasks WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2;   -- 42, 123
```

One row comes back, so the server replies:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"id": 42, "title": "Buy milk", "done": false,
 "due_date": "2026-10-20", "created_at": "2026-10-14T09:00:00Z"}
```

For `GET /v1/tasks/999` the same SELECT returns **zero rows**. That is not a database error; the query worked and found nothing. The server must turn "no row" into:

```http
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/json

{"error": "task_not_found"}
```

The same happens if Bob asks for Alice's task 42: the `owner_id` condition filters it out, so Bob gets 404.

metadata.source: Adapted from PostgreSQL Documentation — Tutorial: The SQL Language, Creating a New Table, Populating a Table With Rows, Querying a Table, Updates, Deletions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-sql.html) (PostgreSQL Licence); MDN Web Docs — CRUD (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/CRUD), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.section: Worked example: GET /tasks with ordering and limits
chunks.text:
Tables and CRUD — Worked example: GET /tasks with ordering and limits

Alice lists her tasks, newest first, 20 at a time.

```http
GET /v1/tasks?limit=20&offset=0 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...
```

```sql
SELECT id, title, done, due_date, created_at
FROM tasks
WHERE owner_id = $1                 -- 123
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT $2 OFFSET $3;                 -- 20, 0
```

- **ORDER BY**: without it PostgreSQL guarantees no row order, so pages could shuffle between calls. The second key `id DESC` breaks ties when two tasks share a `created_at`, making the order fully determined.
- **LIMIT** caps the rows returned; the server should also enforce a maximum (say 100) so nobody requests a million rows.
- **OFFSET** skips rows for the next page (`offset=20`).

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"items": [{"id": 42, "title": "Buy milk", "done": false}], "limit": 20, "offset": 0}
```

An empty list is still 200 with `"items": []`, not 404: the collection exists, it is just empty.

chunks.section: Worked example: PUT /tasks/{id} replaces the task
chunks.text:
Tables and CRUD — Worked example: PUT /tasks/{id} replaces the task

PUT sends the full new state of the task. Every editable column is set.

```http
PUT /v1/tasks/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...
Content-Type: application/json

{"title": "Buy oat milk", "done": false, "due_date": null}
```

```sql
UPDATE tasks
SET title = $1, done = $2, due_date = $3   -- 'Buy oat milk', false, NULL
WHERE id = $4 AND owner_id = $5            -- 42, 123
RETURNING id, title, done, due_date, created_at;
```

Check the row count. One row updated:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"id": 42, "title": "Buy oat milk", "done": false,
 "due_date": null, "created_at": "2026-10-14T09:00:00Z"}
```

Zero rows updated means no task 42 belongs to Alice, so the answer is 404 Not Found. Note that `id`, `owner_id` and `created_at` are never taken from the body: the client cannot reassign a task to someone else by sending `"owner_id": 456`.

chunks.section: Worked example: PATCH /tasks/{id} updates some columns
chunks.text:
Tables and CRUD — Worked example: PATCH /tasks/{id} updates some columns

PATCH changes only the fields that are present. Alice ticks the task off:

```http
PATCH /v1/tasks/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...
Content-Type: application/json

{"done": true}
```

The server builds the SET list from the fields present in the body, using only column names from a fixed allow-list (`title`, `done`, `due_date`). Values still go in as placeholders:

```sql
UPDATE tasks SET done = $1           -- true
WHERE id = $2 AND owner_id = $3      -- 42, 123
RETURNING id, title, done, due_date, created_at;
```

`title` and `due_date` are not mentioned, so they keep their values. If the body were `{"title": "Buy bread", "due_date": null}`, the SET list would be `title = $1, due_date = $2`. An empty body or an unknown field such as `"owner_id"` is rejected with 400 Bad Request. As with PUT: one row updated gives 200 with the task; zero rows gives 404.

chunks.text:
Tables and CRUD — Worked example: DELETE /tasks/{id}

Alice deletes task 42.

```http
DELETE /v1/tasks/42 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...
```

```sql
DELETE FROM tasks
WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2;     -- 42, 123
```

The database reports `DELETE 1`: one row removed. There is nothing useful to send back, so:

```http
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
```

If Alice sends the same request again, the statement reports `DELETE 0`. No row matched, so the server replies 404 Not Found. (Some APIs reply 204 again because the end state, "task 42 is gone", is the same; TaskFlow chooses 404 so clients learn the id was wrong. Pick one rule and document it.)

Never let the `WHERE` clause become empty: `DELETE FROM tasks;` removes every task of every user, immediately and without asking.

chunks.text:
Tables and CRUD — Endpoint-to-SQL map

The whole TaskFlow API on one page (`me` = the authenticated user's id):

```
Endpoint              SQL                                          Success  No row
--------------------  -------------------------------------------  -------  ------
POST   /tasks         INSERT INTO tasks ... RETURNING ...          201      -
GET    /tasks         SELECT ... WHERE owner_id=me ORDER BY LIMIT  200      200 []
GET    /tasks/{id}    SELECT ... WHERE id=$1 AND owner_id=me       200      404
PUT    /tasks/{id}    UPDATE ... SET all fields WHERE id, owner    200      404
PATCH  /tasks/{id}    UPDATE ... SET given fields WHERE id, owner  200      404
DELETE /tasks/{id}    DELETE ... WHERE id=$1 AND owner_id=me       204      404
POST   /login         SELECT id, password_hash FROM users          200      401
                      WHERE email=$1
```

For `POST /login`, zero rows (unknown email) and a wrong password must both give the same 401 Unauthorized, so attackers cannot learn which emails are registered. Invalid input on any endpoint gives 400 before any SQL runs.

chunks.text:
Tables and CRUD — When no row matches

A beginner trap: a SQL statement that matches nothing **succeeds**. It does not throw an error. Your code has to look at the result and decide.

- `SELECT` returns zero rows → the resource does not exist (for this user) → **404 Not Found**.
- `UPDATE` reports 0 rows affected → nothing was changed → **404 Not Found**.
- `DELETE` reports 0 rows affected → nothing was deleted → **404 Not Found**.
- A list `SELECT` that returns zero rows → **200 OK** with an empty list.

In pseudocode:

```
row = db.query("UPDATE tasks SET done = $1 WHERE id = $2 AND owner_id = $3 RETURNING ...",
               [true, 42, me])
if row is empty:
    return 404 {"error": "task_not_found"}
return 200 row
```

Do not run a SELECT first "to check it exists" and then the UPDATE: it doubles the work, and the row could be deleted in between. Run the change once and read the row count.

metadata.source: Adapted from PostgreSQL Documentation — Tutorial: The SQL Language, Creating a New Table, Populating a Table With Rows, Querying a Table, Updates, Deletions (https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial-sql.html) (PostgreSQL Licence); MDN Web Docs — CRUD (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/CRUD), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.text:
Tables and CRUD — NULL versus missing

These look similar in JSON but mean different things:

- **Missing**: the field is absent. `{"done": true}` says nothing about `due_date`.
- **null**: the field is present with no value. `{"due_date": null}` says "remove the due date".

In SQL, `NULL` means "no value". It is not zero, not `false` and not an empty string, and `NULL = NULL` is not true: test with `due_date IS NULL`.

For **PATCH** the difference is crucial:

```
{"done": true}            ->  UPDATE tasks SET done = true ...      (due_date kept)
{"due_date": null}        ->  UPDATE tasks SET due_date = NULL ...  (due_date cleared)
```

A common shortcut, `SET due_date = COALESCE($1, due_date)`, keeps the old value whenever the parameter is NULL. That makes it impossible to clear a due date, because null and missing become the same thing. For **PUT**, a missing optional field is usually treated as null, since PUT replaces the whole task. NOT NULL columns such as `title` must reject null with 400.
