chunks.section: The five classes and the 4xx/5xx rule
chunks.text:
Status Codes and Responses — The five classes and the 4xx/5xx rule

The first digit gives the class.

| Class | Meaning | TaskFlow example |
|---|---|---|
| 1xx Informational | Interim reply; keep going | Rare in APIs |
| 2xx Success | Request received, understood, accepted | Task fetched |
| 3xx Redirection | Further action needed, often a new URL | API moved to /v2 |
| 4xx Client error | The request was wrong or can't be fulfilled as sent | Missing title |
| 5xx Server error | The server failed on a valid request | Database crashed |

The key rule: **4xx means the client must change something. 5xx means the server failed.** After a 4xx, sending the exact same request again will fail again. The client has to fix the body, log in, or pick another URL. After a 5xx, the request itself may be fine, so retrying later can work. This rule also tells you who gets paged at 3 a.m.: a spike of 5xx is the backend team's problem.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes; 201 Created; 401 Unauthorized; 403 Forbidden; 404 Not Found; 409 Conflict; 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.text:
Status Codes and Responses — Success codes: 200, 201, 204

- **200 OK**: the request succeeded. What "success" means depends on the method. For `GET /tasks/42` the body holds the task. For `PUT` or `PATCH` it usually holds the updated task.
- **201 Created**: the request succeeded **and a new resource was created**, typically after `POST`. Send a `Location` header with the URL of the new resource. Usually the body also holds the created object.
- **204 No Content**: success, and there is deliberately **no body**. This is common for `DELETE /tasks/42`, or for an update when the client doesn't need the result back.

```http
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: https://api.taskflow.example/v1/tasks/43
Content-Type: application/json

{"id": 43, "title": "Pay rent", "done": false}
```

Pick the most specific one. "Created" says more than "OK", and the `Location` header lets the client find the new task without guessing its id.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes; 201 Created; 401 Unauthorized; 403 Forbidden; 404 Not Found; 409 Conflict; 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.text:
Status Codes and Responses — Redirects: 301 and 304 (briefly)

You will meet two 3xx codes in APIs.

- **301 Moved Permanently**: the resource's URL has changed for good. The new URL goes in the `Location` header. If TaskFlow retires `/v1/todo-items`, it can answer `301` with `Location: /v1/tasks`. Clients should then update their stored URL.
- **304 Not Modified**: used with caching. The client says "I have a copy from earlier" (for example with an `If-None-Match` header carrying an ETag). The server answers `304` with **no body**, meaning "nothing changed, keep using your cached copy". This saves bandwidth when the app refreshes the task list and nothing has changed.

```http
GET /v1/tasks/42 HTTP/1.1
If-None-Match: "v7"

HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified
ETag: "v7"
```

Beginners rarely send these by hand, but you should recognise them in logs.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes; 201 Created; 401 Unauthorized; 403 Forbidden; 404 Not Found; 409 Conflict; 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.text:
Status Codes and Responses — Client errors: 400, 404, 405

- **400 Bad Request**: the server can't or won't process the request because of a client error, usually **malformed syntax**. Examples are broken JSON (`{"title": "Buy milk",}`) or a query parameter that can't be parsed.
- **404 Not Found**: the server cannot find the requested resource. In an API, the endpoint can be perfectly valid while the specific item doesn't exist, as in `GET /tasks/999` when there is no task 999. A 404 does not say whether the absence is temporary or permanent. (`410 Gone` exists for "deleted for good".)
- **405 Method Not Allowed**: the URL exists, but it doesn't support this method. For example, TaskFlow has no `DELETE /tasks` for wiping the whole collection. The response should include an `Allow` header listing what *is* supported:

```http
HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed
Allow: GET, POST
```

Notice the difference: 404 means "nothing lives at this address". 405 means "something lives here, but you can't do that to it".

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes; 201 Created; 401 Unauthorized; 403 Forbidden; 404 Not Found; 409 Conflict; 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.text:
Status Codes and Responses — 401 vs 403: the most confused pair

The names are misleading, so learn the meanings.

- **401 Unauthorized** really means **unauthenticated**. The request lacks valid credentials, because the token is missing, expired or invalid. The server doesn't know who you are. Logging in and retrying can fix it. A 401 should come with a `WWW-Authenticate` header naming the expected scheme, such as `WWW-Authenticate: Bearer`.
- **403 Forbidden** means **authenticated but not allowed**. The server knows exactly who you are, and the answer is still no. Logging in again won't help.

Quick test: *would a fresh, valid login change the outcome?* If yes, use 401. If no, use 403.

In TaskFlow, a request with no `Authorization` header gets 401. Bob, with a valid token, trying to delete Alice's task gets 403. Some servers deliberately return 404 instead of 403 to hide that the resource exists at all. That is an accepted privacy choice.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes; 201 Created; 401 Unauthorized; 403 Forbidden; 404 Not Found; 409 Conflict; 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.text:
Status Codes and Responses — Client errors: 409, 422, 429

- **409 Conflict**: the request conflicts with the **current state** of the resource. Examples: registering with an email that's already taken, or two people editing the same task at once when the client's version is out of date. The body should explain the conflict so the client can resolve it and resubmit.
- **422 Unprocessable Content**: the body was **parsed fine**, but its content fails the rules. Valid JSON with `"due_date": "yesterday"`, or an empty title, is a typical case. Remember **400 = can't read it, 422 = read it, but it's not acceptable**. Some APIs use 400 for both, but if you use 422, use it consistently.
- **429 Too Many Requests**: the client sent too many requests in a given time (rate limiting). Include `Retry-After: 30` so the client knows how long to wait.

All three are still 4xx. The client must change something: resolve the conflict, fix the data, or slow down.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes; 201 Created; 401 Unauthorized; 403 Forbidden; 404 Not Found; 409 Conflict; 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.text:
Status Codes and Responses — Server errors: 500, 503

- **500 Internal Server Error**: a generic error. The server hit a situation it doesn't know how to handle, like an unhandled exception, a bug, or a null pointer. The client did nothing wrong. Never put stack traces or SQL in the body, because they leak internals to attackers. Log the details on the server and return a short message, ideally with a request id for support.
- **503 Service Unavailable**: the server is **temporarily** unable to handle the request, for example during maintenance, overload, or when the database is down. It should be temporary, and a `Retry-After` header can say when to try again.

```http
HTTP/1.1 503 Service Unavailable
Retry-After: 120
Content-Type: application/json

{"error": "maintenance", "message": "TaskFlow is upgrading. Back in 2 minutes."}
```

A 5xx is never the user's fault. If your API returns 500 for a missing title, that's a bug: it should be 422 or 400.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes; 201 Created; 401 Unauthorized; 403 Forbidden; 404 Not Found; 409 Conflict; 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.section: Choosing the code: a decision flow
chunks.text:
Status Codes and Responses — Choosing the code: a decision flow

Walk through these questions in order and stop at the first "yes".

```text
1. Did the server itself fail (crash, DB down, overload)?
      crash/bug -> 500     temporarily down/overloaded -> 503
2. Is the client sending too fast?                     -> 429
3. Can't parse the request (bad JSON, bad syntax)?     -> 400
4. No valid credentials (missing/expired token)?       -> 401
5. Does the URL point to nothing?                      -> 404
6. URL exists but the method isn't supported?          -> 405
7. Known user, but not allowed to do this?             -> 403
8. Parsed fine, but data breaks validation rules?      -> 422
9. Clashes with current state (duplicate, stale)?      -> 409
10. Success:
      created something -> 201 + Location
      nothing to return -> 204
      otherwise         -> 200
```

Real servers check authentication early, so 401 often comes before 404. That way an anonymous caller can't probe which task ids exist. The order is a guide, not a law. What matters is that each code matches what actually happened.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes; 201 Created; 401 Unauthorized; 403 Forbidden; 404 Not Found; 409 Conflict; 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.section: Response bodies and headers that go with each code
chunks.text:
Status Codes and Responses — Response bodies and headers that go with each code

Each code has a typical companion.

| Code | Body | Header to send |
|---|---|---|
| 200 | The resource or result | `Content-Type` |
| 201 | The created resource | `Location` |
| 204 | None, ever | |
| 304 | None | `ETag` |
| 401 | Short error | `WWW-Authenticate` |
| 405 | Short error | `Allow` |
| 429, 503 | Short error | `Retry-After` |
| other 4xx/5xx | Error object | `Content-Type` |

Use **one error shape** across the whole API so clients can parse every failure the same way:

```json
{
  "error": "validation_failed",
  "message": "The request body has invalid fields.",
  "details": [{"field": "title", "issue": "must not be empty"}]
}
```

The `error` field is a stable machine-readable code. `message` is for humans. `details` points at the exact field the client must change.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes; 201 Created; 401 Unauthorized; 403 Forbidden; 404 Not Found; 409 Conflict; 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.text:
Status Codes and Responses — Worked example: Creating a task

Alice (user 123) creates a task.

```http
POST /v1/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...
Content-Type: application/json

{"title": "Pay rent", "due_date": "2026-11-01"}
```

Step 1: Credentials are valid, so not 401. Step 2: The JSON parses, so not 400. Step 3: The title is non-empty and the date is real, so not 422. Step 4: The server inserts a row:

```sql
INSERT INTO tasks (owner_id, title, done, due_date, created_at)
VALUES (123, 'Pay rent', false, '2026-11-01', now())
RETURNING id;   -- returns 43
```

Step 5: Something new exists, so the answer is **201**, with its URL:

```http
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Location: https://api.taskflow.example/v1/tasks/43
Content-Type: application/json

{"id": 43, "owner_id": 123, "title": "Pay rent", "done": false,
 "due_date": "2026-11-01", "created_at": "2026-10-14T09:12:00Z"}
```

Why not 200? 200 would work, but 201 tells the client precisely that a task was created and where to find it.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes; 201 Created; 401 Unauthorized; 403 Forbidden; 404 Not Found; 409 Conflict; 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.section: Worked example: Deleting a task twice
chunks.text:
Status Codes and Responses — Worked example: Deleting a task twice

Alice deletes task 43.

```http
DELETE /v1/tasks/43 HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...

HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
```

The task is gone and there's nothing useful to return, so the answer is **204** with an empty body. (A `200` with a small confirmation body is also acceptable. Just be consistent.)

Her app has a flaky connection and sends the same `DELETE` again:

```http
DELETE /v1/tasks/43 HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/json

{"error": "task_not_found", "message": "Task 43 does not exist."}
```

Now the task doesn't exist, so **404** is honest. The app can treat "404 on delete" as "already gone". Then she tries `DELETE /v1/tasks` (the whole collection). TaskFlow doesn't support that, so the answer is **405** with `Allow: GET, POST`.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes; 201 Created; 401 Unauthorized; 403 Forbidden; 404 Not Found; 409 Conflict; 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.section: Worked example: Bob and Alice's task
chunks.text:
Status Codes and Responses — Worked example: Bob and Alice's task

Task 42 belongs to Alice (owner_id 123). Three requests arrive.

**(a) No token at all:**

```http
GET /v1/tasks/42 HTTP/1.1

HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer
```

The server doesn't know who this is. Logging in could fix it, so the answer is **401**.

**(b) Bob (user 456) with a valid token:**

```http
DELETE /v1/tasks/42 HTTP/1.1
Authorization: Bearer <Bob's valid token>

HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
Content-Type: application/json

{"error": "forbidden", "message": "You can only delete your own tasks."}
```

The server knows it's Bob and checks `owner_id = 456`. That doesn't match 123. A new login won't change that, so the answer is **403**. (TaskFlow could choose 404 here to hide that task 42 exists.)

**(c) Bob's token has expired:** the answer is **401** again. Identity can't be confirmed, and refreshing the token fixes it.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes; 201 Created; 401 Unauthorized; 403 Forbidden; 404 Not Found; 409 Conflict; 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.section: Worked example: Bad JSON vs bad data
chunks.text:
Status Codes and Responses — Worked example: Bad JSON vs bad data

Alice's app sends two broken requests.

**Request 1:** broken syntax, with a trailing comma.

```http
POST /v1/tasks HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"title": "Call mum",}
```

The server can't even parse it, so the answer is **400 Bad Request**: `{"error": "invalid_json", "message": "Unexpected '}' at position 21."}`

**Request 2:** perfect JSON, impossible content.

```http
POST /v1/tasks HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/json

{"title": "", "due_date": "2026-02-30"}
```

It parses fine, but the title is empty and February 30 doesn't exist. The answer is **422**, pointing at the fields:

```json
{"error": "validation_failed",
 "details": [{"field": "title", "issue": "must not be empty"},
             {"field": "due_date", "issue": "not a real date"}]}
```

In both cases the client must change the request. That's why both are 4xx. Only the kind of fix differs.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes; 201 Created; 401 Unauthorized; 403 Forbidden; 404 Not Found; 409 Conflict; 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.section: Common mistake: 200 OK with an error inside
chunks.text:
Status Codes and Responses — Common mistake: 200 OK with an error inside

**Mistake:**

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{"success": false, "error": "Task not found"}
```

**Why it's wrong:** the status line says "it worked" and the body says "it didn't". Every layer that only looks at the code now believes the request succeeded. HTTP libraries won't raise an error, monitoring dashboards show 100% success, retry logic never runs, and caches may store the "error" as a valid answer. Each client has to invent its own way to dig the truth out of the body.

**Correct version:** let the code tell the truth and keep the body for details.

```http
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/json

{"error": "task_not_found", "message": "Task 999 does not exist."}
```

Rule of thumb: if the body contains the word "error", the status code should not be 2xx.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes; 201 Created; 401 Unauthorized; 403 Forbidden; 404 Not Found; 409 Conflict; 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.text:
Status Codes and Responses — Common mistakes: other mix-ups

- **401 for "not your task".** Bob is logged in, so this is 403 (or 404 to hide the task). 401 would make his app wrongly show a login screen.
- **500 for bad input.** An empty title crashing the server into a 500 is a bug. Validate input and return 422 (or 400). A 5xx should mean "our fault".
- **200 for creation without a Location.** Prefer 201 plus `Location: .../tasks/43`.
- **A body on 204.** 204 means no content. If you want to return the task, use 200.
- **404 for a wrong method.** If `/tasks` exists but `DELETE` isn't supported, that's 405 with `Allow`.
- **Leaking internals on 500.** Don't send stack traces or SQL errors to the client. Log them and send a short message with a request id.
- **Retrying a 4xx unchanged.** The same request will fail the same way. Retry 503 and 429 after `Retry-After`. Fix the request for other 4xx.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes; 201 Created; 401 Unauthorized; 403 Forbidden; 404 Not Found; 409 Conflict; 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.text:
Status Codes and Responses — Summary

- A status code is the machine-readable headline of a response. Clients act on it first.
- Classes: 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.
- **4xx = the client must change something. 5xx = the server failed.**
- Success: 200 (OK), 201 (created, plus `Location`), 204 (no body).
- Redirects: 301 (moved, plus `Location`), 304 (use your cached copy).
- Client errors: 400 (unparseable), 401 (not authenticated), 403 (authenticated but not allowed), 404 (doesn't exist), 405 (method not supported, plus `Allow`), 409 (conflicts with current state), 422 (parsed but invalid), 429 (too many, plus `Retry-After`).
- Server errors: 500 (unexpected failure), 503 (temporarily unavailable, plus `Retry-After`).
- Never return 200 with an error body. Use one consistent error shape.
- Choose the code by asking what actually happened, using the decision flow.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes; 201 Created; 401 Unauthorized; 403 Forbidden; 404 Not Found; 409 Conflict; 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.text:
Status Codes and Responses — Exercise: Choose the status code

For each TaskFlow situation, give the status code, one important header (if any), and a one-sentence justification:

1. Alice sends `PATCH /v1/tasks/42` with `{"done": true}`, and the server returns the updated task.
2. Alice sends `POST /v1/tasks` with valid JSON whose `due_date` is `"next-ish week"`.
3. Bob, logged in, sends `GET /v1/tasks/42`, which belongs to Alice.
4. A script sends 500 requests in ten seconds and TaskFlow's limit is 100 per minute.
5. The PostgreSQL server is down for scheduled maintenance.

Then explain in two or three sentences why situations 2 and 5 belong to different classes.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes; 201 Created; 401 Unauthorized; 403 Forbidden; 404 Not Found; 409 Conflict; 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.text:
Status Codes and Responses — Exercise: Fix the error responses

A junior developer wrote TaskFlow's error handling so that every response is `200 OK`, with bodies like `{"success": false, "error": "not logged in"}`, `{"success": false, "error": "task not found"}` and `{"success": false, "error": "database timeout"}`.

Explain what problems this causes for a mobile app, for monitoring, and for automatic retries. Then rewrite each of the three responses with the correct status code, any header that should go with it, and a body in a consistent error format.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — HTTP response status codes; 201 Created; 401 Unauthorized; 403 Forbidden; 404 Not Found; 409 Conflict; 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Responses — Why this matters

Think of a post office counter. The clerk checks that your parcel has an address, a stamp, and is not too heavy before accepting it. If something is wrong, the clerk tells you exactly what to fix: "the postcode is missing". The clerk does not quietly guess a postcode, and does not hand you the sorting office's internal paperwork.

An API is that counter, and every request is a parcel from a stranger. Validation is the check; the error response is what the clerk says when refusing. Weak validation lets bad data into the database (a task with no title, a due date of "banana"). Weak error responses leave clients unable to fix mistakes, or tell attackers how the server is built. This unit covers both: what to check, and how to say "no" clearly and safely.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — 400 Bad Request (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/400) and 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/422), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5; OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html) and OWASP Error Handling Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Error_Handling_Cheat_Sheet.html), CC BY-SA 4.0. Reference (not copied): RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457), © IETF Trust.

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Responses — Never trust input

**Input** is anything the client controls: the JSON body, the URL path (`/tasks/42`), query parameters (`?done=true`), and headers. The server must treat all of it as untrusted.

A common beginner thought is: "The TaskFlow web form already stops empty titles, so the server doesn't need to." That is wrong. Client-side checks (in the browser or mobile app) exist to **help honest users** with instant feedback. They do not **protect the server**, because anyone can skip the form entirely:

```bash
curl -X POST https://api.taskflow.example/v1/tasks \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title": ""}'
```

This request never touched the form. OWASP's rule: validate on the server even when the browser checks the same fields. Browser checks are for usability; server checks are for protection.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — 400 Bad Request (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/400) and 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/422), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5; OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html) and OWASP Error Handling Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Error_Handling_Cheat_Sheet.html), CC BY-SA 4.0. Reference (not copied): RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457), © IETF Trust.

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Responses — What to validate for TaskFlow

Write the rules down per field before writing any code. For `POST /tasks`:

| Field | Rule |
|---|---|
| `title` | Required. A string. 1–200 characters after trimming spaces. |
| `due_date` | Optional. A string in `YYYY-MM-DD` form that is a real calendar date (no `2026-02-30`) and is in the future. |
| `done` | Optional, default `false`. Must be a JSON boolean: `true` or `false`, not `"yes"` or `1`. |
| anything else | Not allowed. `id`, `owner_id` and `created_at` are set by the server. |

OWASP distinguishes two levels. **Syntactic** validation checks type and format: is `due_date` shaped like a date? **Semantic** validation checks meaning: is that date in the future? Both are needed. A type check alone only proves a value is the right kind of thing, not that it is acceptable. Note also that `owner_id` is never read from the body; the server takes it from the authenticated user.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — 400 Bad Request (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/400) and 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/422), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5; OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html) and OWASP Error Handling Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Error_Handling_Cheat_Sheet.html), CC BY-SA 4.0. Reference (not copied): RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457), © IETF Trust.

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Responses — Allowlist validation

There are two ways to write rules.

- **Denylist**: list what is forbidden ("reject titles containing `<script>`") and accept everything else. Attackers only need one input you didn't think of.
- **Allowlist**: list exactly what is permitted and reject everything else. OWASP recommends this: define what you accept instead of trying to recognise every malicious string.

For TaskFlow, the allowlist is the table from the previous section. The body may contain only `title`, `done` and `due_date`; each must have the stated type, length or range. A body with an extra `owner_id` field fails the allowlist, so a sneaky client cannot assign a task to someone else.

Allowlisting does not replace other defences. A valid title can still contain an apostrophe, so SQL must still use parameterised queries:

```sql
INSERT INTO tasks (owner_id, title, done, due_date)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4) RETURNING id, created_at;
```

chunks.section: Validate early, reject, don't silently fix
chunks.text:
Validation and Error Responses — Validate early, reject, don't silently fix

**Validate early** means checking the request at the edge of the server, before any business logic or database work. OWASP adds that size limits should apply even before the body is parsed, so a 500 MB body is refused without being read.

**Reject, don't silently fix** means that if input is wrong, the server says so and changes nothing. Tempting "helpful" fixes cause real bugs:

- Cutting a 250-character title down to 200: the user loses text without knowing.
- Turning `"done": "yes"` into `true`: what would `"maybe"` become?
- Replacing a past due date with today: the user's plan is now wrong.

A clear rejection lets the client fix the real problem. Also, reject the whole request, not part of it: OWASP advises against processing invalid requests partially. Either the task is created exactly as asked, or nothing is created and the client gets an explanation.

```text
parse body -> check allowlist -> check each field -> only then INSERT
```

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Responses — 400 vs 422

Two status codes cover most bad request bodies.

- **400 Bad Request**: the server cannot even understand the request. MDN gives malformed syntax as the classic cause, for example JSON with a trailing comma. The server cannot read the fields at all.
- **422 Unprocessable Content**: the request is well-formed (correct content type, valid JSON) but the values inside break the rules, such as an empty title or a past due date. The code began in WebDAV and is now part of core HTTP semantics (RFC 9110).

| Body sent | Problem | TaskFlow returns |
|---|---|---|
| `{"title": "Buy milk",}` | not valid JSON | 400 |
| `{"title": ""}` | valid JSON, invalid value | 422 |

Be aware that many well-known APIs use 400 for both cases, and that is also acceptable. What matters is that the API documents its choice and is consistent. In both cases, MDN notes that repeating the identical request will fail again: the client must change it first.

chunks.section: Worked example: a missing task vs an empty list
chunks.text:
Validation and Error Responses — Worked example: a missing task vs an empty list

**Step 1. A specific item.** Alice asks for task 99999, which does not exist. **404 Not Found** means "the thing you named does not exist":

```http
GET /v1/tasks/99999 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...

HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"type": "https://api.taskflow.example/problems/not-found",
 "title": "Resource not found", "status": 404,
 "detail": "No task with id 99999 exists."}
```

**Step 2. A collection.** `GET /tasks?done=true` asks "list my finished tasks". If Alice has none, the collection still exists; it is just empty:

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

[]
```

**Step 3. The rule.** A missing *item* is 404; a filter that matches nothing is 200 with `[]`. A 404 there would make clients treat "no results" as an error.

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Responses — 409 Conflict

**409 Conflict** means the request is valid on its own but clashes with the current state of the server. Nothing is wrong with the fields; the problem is what already exists.

Example: suppose TaskFlow adds a sign-up endpoint and `bob@example.com` is already registered (user 456). A new request tries to register the same email:

```http
POST /v1/users HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Content-Type: application/json

{"email": "bob@example.com", "name": "Robert", "password": "..."}

HTTP/1.1 409 Conflict
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"type": "https://api.taskflow.example/problems/email-taken",
 "title": "Email already registered", "status": 409,
 "detail": "An account with this email already exists."}
```

Compare with 422: `"email": "not-an-email"` is invalid by itself (422). `"bob@example.com"` is perfectly valid but conflicts with an existing row (409). In the database, a `UNIQUE` constraint on `users.email` is the final safety net that catches this.

Reference (not copied): RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457), © IETF Trust.

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Responses — 405, 413 and 415

Three more codes appear at the edge of the server.

**405 Method Not Allowed**: the URL exists but does not support that method. TaskFlow has no "delete all tasks" operation, so `DELETE /tasks` gets 405. The response must include an `Allow` header listing the methods that do work:

```http
HTTP/1.1 405 Method Not Allowed
Allow: GET, POST
```

**413 Content Too Large**: the body is bigger than the server accepts. TaskFlow might cap bodies at 100 KB; a task never needs more. This is "validate early" in action, refused before parsing.

**415 Unsupported Media Type**: the body's format is not one the server handles. TaskFlow accepts `Content-Type: application/json`; a request sent as `text/plain` or `application/xml` gets 415.

None of these depend on the field values, so the server can check them before looking inside the body.

chunks.section: 500 errors: log inside, say little outside
chunks.text:
Validation and Error Responses — 500 errors: log inside, say little outside

**500 Internal Server Error** means the server failed, not the client. Example: the database is down when Alice creates a task. The client did nothing wrong, so a 4xx would be a lie.

OWASP's guidance: catch unexpected errors in one global handler, log the full details on the server, and return a generic message. Never send this to the client:

```text
ERROR: relation "tasks" does not exist at character 13
  at PgPool.query (/srv/taskflow/db.js:41)
```

That leaks the database type, table names and file paths, all useful to an attacker. Instead:

```http
HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"type": "about:blank", "title": "Internal Server Error",
 "status": 500, "detail": "Something went wrong on our side. Please try again later.",
 "instance": "/errors/7f3a9c"}
```

The server log stores the stack trace under reference `7f3a9c`, so support staff can find it if Alice reports the error. OWASP also advises monitoring 5xx rates: a spike can mean some input is crashing the server.

chunks.section: A consistent error body: Problem Details
chunks.text:
Validation and Error Responses — A consistent error body: Problem Details

If every endpoint invents its own error shape, clients need special code for each. **RFC 9457, Problem Details for HTTP APIs**, defines one standard JSON shape, served with `Content-Type: application/problem+json`. Its members:

- `type`: a URI identifying the *kind* of problem; clients act on this. Omitted, it means `about:blank` (a generic problem described by the status code).
- `title`: a short human summary of that kind of problem; the same every time it occurs.
- `status`: the HTTP status code, repeated; it must match the real status line.
- `detail`: a human explanation of *this* occurrence, aimed at helping the client fix it. Clients should not parse it.
- `instance`: a URI identifying this specific occurrence, such as an error reference.

A problem type may add **extension members**. RFC 9457's validation example adds an `errors` array, one entry per broken field, each with a `detail` and a JSON Pointer `pointer` such as `#/title`. Clients ignore extensions they don't know. TaskFlow uses this shape for all 4xx and 5xx responses.

Reference (not copied): RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457), © IETF Trust.

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Responses — Messages that help without leaking

A good error message tells an honest client what to change, and tells an attacker nothing useful about the internals.

| Helpful and safe | Leaky or useless |
|---|---|
| "title must be 1–200 characters; got 250." | "Error." |
| "due_date must be a future date in YYYY-MM-DD form." | "Invalid input." |
| "Unknown field: owner_id." | "column owner_id violates foreign key constraint fk_users" |
| "No task with id 99999 exists." | "SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE id=99999 returned 0 rows" |

Guidelines:

- Name the field and the rule; give the allowed range or format.
- Never include SQL, stack traces, library versions, file paths or server names. RFC 9457's security section also warns to vet what problem details reveal.
- Be careful about echoing input back; it can end up displayed in a web page.
- For login, keep messages vague on purpose ("email or password is incorrect") so attackers cannot discover which emails are registered.

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Responses — Worked example: malformed JSON

Alice's app has a bug and sends a body with a trailing comma.

```http
POST /v1/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...
Content-Type: application/json

{"title": "Buy milk", "done": false,}
```

**Step 1. Can the server parse it?** No. A trailing comma is not legal JSON, so the server cannot know which fields were sent. Field rules cannot even run.

**Step 2. Choose the status.** The body is malformed, so 400 Bad Request.

**Step 3. Write the body.**

```http
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"type": "https://api.taskflow.example/problems/malformed-json",
 "title": "Request body is not valid JSON",
 "status": 400,
 "detail": "The body could not be parsed as JSON near character 36. Check for trailing commas or missing quotes."}
```

**Step 4. Side effects.** None. No row is inserted. Note the message gives a position and a hint but does not quote the parser's internal exception text.

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Responses — Worked example: invalid field values

Now the JSON is valid, but two values break the rules (today is 2026-10-14):

```json
{"title": "", "due_date": "2025-01-10", "done": false}
```

**Step 1. Parse.** Succeeds, so this is not a 400.
**Step 2. Allowlist.** Only allowed fields are present. Good.
**Step 3. Field rules.** `title` is empty (needs 1–200 chars). `due_date` is in the past. `done` is fine.
**Step 4. Respond with every field error at once**, so the client fixes both in one go:

```http
HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Content
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"type": "https://api.taskflow.example/problems/validation-error",
 "title": "Your request is not valid",
 "status": 422,
 "detail": "2 fields failed validation.",
 "errors": [
   {"pointer": "#/title", "detail": "must be 1-200 characters"},
   {"pointer": "#/due_date", "detail": "must be a future date"}
 ]}
```

The `errors` array is the RFC 9457 extension pattern. An API that uses 400 for all validation would send the same body with status 400.

metadata.source: Adapted from MDN Web Docs — 400 Bad Request (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/400) and 422 Unprocessable Content (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Status/422), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5; OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html) and OWASP Error Handling Cheat Sheet (https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Error_Handling_Cheat_Sheet.html), CC BY-SA 4.0. Reference (not copied): RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457), © IETF Trust.

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Responses — Worked example: an unknown field

Third problem: Alice's request is valid JSON with a good title, but includes a field she must not set.

```json
{"title": "Pay rent", "owner_id": 456}
```

**Step 1. Parse.** Fine.
**Step 2. Allowlist.** `owner_id` is not on the list for `POST /tasks`. If the server copied the body straight into the database, Alice could create tasks in Bob's account (a "mass assignment" bug).
**Step 3. Decide.** Some APIs silently ignore unknown fields. TaskFlow rejects them, so mistakes and tampering are visible:

```http
HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Content
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"type": "https://api.taskflow.example/problems/validation-error",
 "title": "Your request is not valid",
 "status": 422,
 "detail": "The body contains fields that are not allowed.",
 "errors": [{"pointer": "#/owner_id", "detail": "unknown or read-only field"}]}
```

**Step 4. Remember the rule.** Even with a correct body, `owner_id` is always taken from the token (Alice, 123), never from the client.

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Responses — Common mistakes

**Mistake: validating only in the browser.** Why wrong: curl or a script bypasses the form. Correct: validate on the server; keep browser checks for usability.

**Mistake: returning 200 with `{"error": "title missing"}`.** Why wrong: clients, caches and monitoring read the status code and think it succeeded. Correct: 422 (or 400) with a Problem Details body.

**Mistake: returning 500 for bad input.** Why wrong: 5xx says the server is broken; it hides client mistakes and triggers false alarms. Correct: input problems are 4xx. A 500 should mean an actual bug or outage.

**Mistake: leaking internals.** Why wrong: a stack trace or SQL message maps your system for attackers. Correct: log details server-side, return a generic message with a reference id.

**Mistake: reporting only the first error.** Why wrong: the client fixes one field, resubmits, and hits the next. Correct: list all field errors in `errors`.

Reference (not copied): RFC 9457 Problem Details for HTTP APIs (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457), © IETF Trust.

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Responses — Summary

- All input (body, path, query, headers) is untrusted. Client-side checks help users; only server-side checks protect the server.
- Write per-field rules (required, type, length, format, range) and validate with an **allowlist**; reject unknown fields such as `owner_id`.
- Validate early, reject the whole request, and never silently "fix" data.
- 400 = malformed (cannot parse); 422 = well-formed but invalid. Many APIs use 400 for both; be consistent and document it.
- 404 = a named item is missing; an empty collection is 200 with `[]`.
- 409 = valid request that clashes with current state. 405 needs an `Allow` header; 413 = body too large; 415 = wrong content type.
- 500 = the server's fault: log details internally, return a generic message.
- Use RFC 9457 Problem Details (`type`, `title`, `status`, `detail`, `instance`) with an `errors` extension for field-level problems.
- Messages should name the field and rule, never SQL, stack traces or paths.

chunks.text:
Validation and Error Responses — Exercise: Respond to three bad requests

Bob (user 456) sends three separate requests to TaskFlow. For each, give the status code you would return, explain why in one or two sentences, and write the Problem Details response body (including an `errors` array where appropriate). Assume today is 2026-10-14.

2. `POST /tasks` with body `{"title": "Call the bank"` (the closing brace is missing)

Validation and Error Responses — Exercise: Review an error-handling design

A teammate's TaskFlow pull request behaves as follows:

chunks.text:
How the Web Works — Why this matters

Every time you open an app, check the weather, or load a web page, two computers have a short conversation. One asks for something; the other answers. A backend engineer builds the side that answers.

Think of a restaurant. You (the customer) do not walk into the kitchen. You tell the waiter what you want, the kitchen prepares it, and the waiter brings it back. You never need to know how the kitchen is organised — only how to order.

The web works the same way. In this course we build the "kitchen" for TaskFlow, a task-management app whose server lives at `https://api.taskflow.example/v1`. Before we can design its API, we need a clear picture of who asks, who answers, how they find each other, and what the messages look like. Everything later in the course — methods, status codes, JSON, authentication — sits on top of the ideas in this unit.

(https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn_web_development/Howto/Web_mechanics/What_is_a_URL), DNS glossary (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/DNS), API glossary (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/API), by Mozilla Contributors, CC BY-SA 2.5

chunks.text:
How the Web Works — Clients and servers

A **client** is the program that starts a conversation by asking for something. Examples: Chrome or Firefox on a laptop, the TaskFlow app on Alice's phone, or a script running on another company's computer.

A **server** is a computer (and the software on it) that waits for requests and answers them. It stores web pages, files, or data — for TaskFlow, the server stores users and tasks in a database.

Key facts:

- The **client always starts**. A server does not suddenly send Alice a page she did not ask for; it responds to requests.
- One server talks to **many clients**. Alice (user 123) and Bob (user 456) both send requests to the same TaskFlow server.
- "Server" describes a **role**, not a special kind of machine. Your own laptop can run a server while you develop.

MDN calls the program acting for the user the **user agent** — usually a browser, but it can also be an app, a command-line tool, or a web crawler.

chunks.text:
How the Web Works — The request–response cycle

All communication on the web follows one pattern, the **request–response cycle**:

1. The client sends a **request**: "Please give me X" or "Please do Y".
2. The server **processes** it: looks things up, checks permissions, changes data.
3. The server sends back a **response**: the result, plus a code saying whether it worked.
4. The cycle ends. The next thing the client wants needs a new request.

Back to the restaurant:

- **You order** ("one pasta, no cheese") — that is the request.
- **The kitchen prepares** the dish — that is the server processing.
- **The waiter brings your order** (or says "sorry, we are out of pasta") — that is the response.

Each order is a complete round trip. If you want dessert, you order again. Requests and responses are individual **messages**, not a continuous stream of data.

chunks.text:
How the Web Works — Mapping the restaurant to HTTP

The language that web clients and servers speak is **HTTP** (Hypertext Transfer Protocol). Here is the restaurant mapped onto it:

| Restaurant | HTTP / TaskFlow |
|---|---|
| Customer | Client (browser, TaskFlow app) |
| Kitchen | Server at `api.taskflow.example` |
| Restaurant address | Domain name, found through DNS |
| "I'd like…" | Method, e.g. `GET` (fetch) or `POST` (create) |
| Which dish | Path, e.g. `/v1/tasks/42` |
| "No cheese, please" | Headers and body (extra details) |
| "Here you go" / "Sorry, sold out" | Status code, e.g. `200 OK` or `404 Not Found` |
| The plate of food | Response body, e.g. JSON |

The waiter is the network: it carries messages but does not decide what to cook. HTTP messages travel over **TCP/IP**, the lower-level rules for moving data across the internet in small chunks called **packets**.

chunks.text:
How the Web Works — What a URL is

A **URL** (Uniform Resource Locator) is the address of one resource on the web. Its general shape is:

```
scheme://host:port/path?query#fragment
```

Take this TaskFlow URL:

```
https://api.taskflow.example/v1/tasks?done=false&sort=due_date
```

- **Scheme** `https` — the protocol to use. HTTPS is HTTP with encryption.
- **Host** (domain) `api.taskflow.example` — which server to contact.
- **Port** — omitted here, so the default is used: 443 for HTTPS, 80 for HTTP.
- **Path** `/v1/tasks` — which resource on that server. Today a path is usually not a real file; the server decides what it means.
- **Query** `?done=false&sort=due_date` — extra key=value parameters, separated by `&`.
- **Fragment** `#...` — points inside a page and is **never sent to the server**.

chunks.text:
How the Web Works — DNS: the internet's address book

Computers find each other using **IP addresses**, numbers like `192.0.2.172`. Humans prefer names like `api.taskflow.example`. The **Domain Name System (DNS)** translates one into the other.

A **DNS lookup** works like looking up a contact on your phone: you tap "Pizza Place" and the phone dials the number stored for it. The client asks a DNS resolver "what is the IP address of `api.taskflow.example`?" and gets back an address it can connect to.

Useful facts:

- DNS is **hierarchical and decentralised** — no single computer holds every name.
- Results are **cached**, so repeated visits skip the lookup.
- Big services may have **several servers**, so the IP you receive can depend on where you are.
- DNS only finds the server. It does not carry your request or know anything about tasks.

chunks.section: What happens when you type a web address
chunks.text:
How the Web Works — What happens when you type a web address

When you type `https://taskflow.example` into a browser and press Enter:

1. **Parse the URL.** The browser splits out scheme `https`, host `taskflow.example`, path `/`.
2. **DNS lookup.** The browser finds the server's IP address (or uses a cached one).
3. **Connect.** It opens a TCP connection to that IP on port 443 and sets up encryption (TLS) because the scheme is HTTPS.
4. **Send the request.** For example `GET / HTTP/1.1` with a `Host: taskflow.example` header.
5. **Server responds.** If all is well: `200 OK` plus an HTML page, sent as a series of packets.
6. **Render.** The browser reassembles the packets, reads the HTML, and sends *more* requests for the CSS, JavaScript, and images the page needs.
7. **Close or reuse** the connection for later requests.

One page view can therefore mean dozens of request–response cycles.

chunks.section: What happens when an app loads data
chunks.text:
How the Web Works — What happens when an app loads data

A mobile app or a JavaScript front end does not want a whole web page. It wants **data**, which it then displays in its own screens.

When Alice opens the TaskFlow app:

1. The app already knows the base URL `https://api.taskflow.example/v1`.
2. It does a DNS lookup for `api.taskflow.example` and connects on port 443.
3. It sends `GET /v1/tasks` with a header proving it is Alice.
4. The server checks who she is, queries the database for tasks where `owner_id = 123`, and builds a reply.
5. The server responds `200 OK` with a **JSON** body — a list of tasks, not HTML.
6. The app turns that JSON into the task list on screen.

The plumbing (DNS, TCP, HTTP) is identical to the browser case. The difference is what travels in the body: structured data meant for a program, not a page meant for a human.

chunks.text:
How the Web Works — HTTP is stateless

HTTP is **stateless**: each request is handled on its own, with no built-in memory of earlier requests — even ones sent over the same connection.

Restaurant version: imagine a waiter with no memory. If you say "same again", they have no idea what you had. You must say the full order every time.

Consequences for TaskFlow:

- Every request must carry **everything the server needs**: who the user is (usually an `Authorization` header) and which resource is meant.
- The server does not "remember" that Alice logged in a minute ago unless she sends proof again.
- Because no request depends on server memory of the previous one, **any** of several identical servers can answer it. This makes scaling much easier.

Stateless does not mean "sessionless". Sites build sessions *on top* of HTTP by having the client resend a cookie or token with each request.

chunks.text:
How the Web Works — What an API is

An **API** (Application Programming Interface) is a set of rules that lets one piece of software use another. A web page is an interface for **people**; an API is an interface for **programs**.

MDN describes an API as a **contract**: the application offering it promises "if you send me a request shaped like this, I will answer like that."

A **web API** is an API reached over HTTP. TaskFlow's API is a list of URLs and methods with agreed meanings:

```
GET    /tasks          list my tasks
POST   /tasks          create a task
GET    /tasks/{id}     read one task
PUT    /tasks/{id}     replace a task
PATCH  /tasks/{id}     change part of a task
DELETE /tasks/{id}     delete a task
POST   /login          sign in
```

The app on Alice's phone does not read HTML; it calls these endpoints and gets JSON back. The word **endpoint** means one method + path combination of an API.

chunks.text:
How the Web Works — Three kinds of clients

The same TaskFlow API can serve very different clients:

- **Browser.** A person visits `https://taskflow.example`. The browser downloads HTML, CSS, and JavaScript; then the JavaScript calls `https://api.taskflow.example/v1/tasks` to fetch data.
- **Mobile app.** The TaskFlow iOS/Android app has its screens built in. It only needs data, so it calls the API directly and receives JSON.
- **Server-to-server.** No human is involved at all. For example, a calendar company's server calls TaskFlow's API every night to copy due dates into users' calendars, or TaskFlow's own server calls an email service's API to send reminders.

To the TaskFlow server these all look the same: an HTTP request arrives, and a response goes back. That is why one well-designed API can support a website, two phone apps, and partner integrations at once.

chunks.section: Worked example: Reading a TaskFlow URL
chunks.text:
How the Web Works — Worked example: Reading a TaskFlow URL

**Problem.** Bob's app requests this URL. Name each part and say what the server receives.

```
https://api.taskflow.example:443/v1/tasks/42?fields=title,done#notes
```

**Step 1 — scheme.** `https`: use HTTP over an encrypted connection.

**Step 2 — host.** `api.taskflow.example`: the client runs a DNS lookup on this name.

**Step 3 — port.** `443`: the default for HTTPS, so writing it is optional.

**Step 4 — path.** `/v1/tasks/42`: version 1 of the API, the tasks collection, task with id 42.

**Step 5 — query.** `fields=title,done`: a parameter asking for only some fields.

**Step 6 — fragment.** `#notes`: stays in the client; it is **not** sent.

**What actually goes over the wire:**

```http
GET /v1/tasks/42?fields=title,done HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
```

Notice the request line holds only path + query; the host travels in the `Host` header, and the fragment is gone.

chunks.section: Worked example: Alice's app loads her tasks
chunks.text:
How the Web Works — Worked example: Alice's app loads her tasks

**Situation.** Alice (user 123) opens TaskFlow on her phone. Trace the exchange.

**Step 1 — DNS.** The phone resolves `api.taskflow.example` to an IP address, say `203.0.113.10`.

**Step 2 — connect.** TCP connection to `203.0.113.10:443`, then TLS encryption.

**Step 3 — request.**

```http
GET /v1/tasks HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Accept: application/json
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...
```

**Step 4 — server work.** It verifies the token belongs to user 123, then runs:

```sql
SELECT id, title, done, due_date FROM tasks WHERE owner_id = 123;
```

**Step 5 — response.**

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

[{"id": 42, "title": "Buy milk", "done": false, "due_date": "2026-10-20"},
 {"id": 43, "title": "Call dentist", "done": true, "due_date": null}]
```

**Step 6 — display.** The app draws two rows. One request, one response, cycle complete.

chunks.text:
How the Web Works — Worked example: Bob's second request

**Situation.** Bob (user 456) signs in, then a moment later opens task 77. His app sends:

```http
GET /v1/tasks/77 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
```

The server replies:

```http
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
Content-Type: application/json

{"error": "missing credentials"}
```

**Why?** Bob is confused: "I just logged in!" But HTTP is stateless. The login was a separate request; this new request contains nothing saying who is asking, so the server must treat it as an anonymous stranger.

**Fix.** The app keeps the token it received from `POST /login` and sends it with **every** request:

```http
GET /v1/tasks/77 HTTP/1.1
Host: api.taskflow.example
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...
```

Now the server can identify user 456 and check that task 77 is his. The rule: each request must stand on its own.

chunks.section: Worked example: Page versus API response
chunks.text:
How the Web Works — Worked example: Page versus API response **Question.** Alice visits `https://taskflow.example/tasks` in a browser, and her phone app calls `https://api.taskflow.example/v1/tasks`. How do the responses differ? **Browser (web page for a human):** ```http HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: text/html

My tasks

  • Buy milk
    • ... ``` The browser renders this into a visible page. The data is mixed with layout. **App (API for a program):** ```http HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: application/json [{"id": 42, "title": "Buy milk", "done": false}] ``` **Analysis.** - Both are HTTP responses with a status line, headers, and a body. - `Content-Type` tells the client what kind of body to expect. - The JSON has no layout; it is pure data that any program can parse and display in its own way. This is the core idea of an API: the server delivers data, and each client decides how to present it.

chunks.section: Worked example: A server as a client
chunks.text:
How the Web Works — Worked example: A server as a client

**Situation.** TaskFlow wants to email Alice when a task is due tomorrow. It uses an email company, MailCo, which offers an API.

**Step 1.** A scheduled job on the TaskFlow server finds due tasks:

```sql
SELECT t.title, u.email FROM tasks t JOIN users u ON u.id = t.owner_id
WHERE t.done = false AND t.due_date = CURRENT_DATE + 1;
```

**Step 2.** For each row, the TaskFlow server — now acting as a **client** — calls MailCo:

```http
POST /v3/send HTTP/1.1
Host: api.mailco.example
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer mc_live_...

{"to": "alice@example.com", "subject": "Due tomorrow: Buy milk"}
```

**Step 3.** MailCo responds `202 Accepted`.

**Lesson.** "Client" and "server" are roles in one conversation. The same machine is a server to Alice's phone and a client to MailCo. No browser or human is involved in Step 2.

chunks.text:
How the Web Works — Common mistakes

**Mistake: "The server pushes pages to me."**
Why it's wrong: in HTTP the client always starts. Correct: the browser or app sends a request; the server only responds.

**Mistake: "DNS sends my request to the server."**
Why it's wrong: DNS only translates a name into an IP address. Correct: after the lookup, the client connects to that IP and sends the HTTP request itself.

**Mistake: "The server remembers I'm logged in."**
Why it's wrong: HTTP is stateless. Correct: the client resends a token or cookie with every request, e.g. `Authorization: Bearer ...`.

**Mistake: "The `#section` part of the URL is sent to the server."**
Why it's wrong: fragments stay in the client. Correct: only the path and query (`/v1/tasks?done=false`) appear in the request line.

**Mistake: "An API is a website."**
Why it's wrong: a website is for people to read; an API is for programs. Correct: an API returns data such as JSON that a client program uses.

chunks.text:
How the Web Works — Summary

- A **client** asks; a **server** answers. The client always starts the conversation.
- Every interaction is a **request–response cycle**: order, kitchen prepares, waiter brings the result.
- **HTTP** is the language of these messages; it travels over **TCP/IP** in packets.
- A **URL** has a scheme, host, optional port, path, query, and fragment; the fragment is never sent.
- **DNS** turns a name like `api.taskflow.example` into an IP address — nothing more.
- Loading a page or app screen means: parse URL → DNS → connect → request → response → display.
- HTTP is **stateless**: each request must carry who you are and what you want.
- An **API** is a contract that lets programs talk to a server; TaskFlow's API returns JSON.
- Browsers, mobile apps, and other servers can all be clients of the same API.
